Conclusion. Joining on the request and job identifiers connects a normal model response to unexpected worker behavior with two blocking decisions. The infrastructure controls observed and stopped those events in this trace without explaining the worker’s intent or proving that no other connection succeeded.

Host sensors, network controls, and the scheduler each observe or enforce their own states, while the join service checks request, job, workload, and time links before correlating them. The measurement reports joined expected events out of all events required by the trace design. Collection consumes storage and processing and may expose operational detail. Missing provider records, clock errors, or an uninstrumented host leave explicit gaps in the joined view.
crumbs: Part V: Testing controls and recovery

title: 15  Failures during live operation
text:
15.2 Attacks, faults, and changed use
A single alarming signal can have several innocent explanations. A runtime indicator is a measurable condition associated with a tested failure path. Examples include access to a forbidden resource, a new external destination, repeated failed tool calls, an abrupt resource increase, or use of stale retrieved content. An indicator needs enough request and system context to separate a likely boundary violation from ordinary variation.
NIST continuous-monitoring guidance says monitoring should support assessment of the security impact of changes and response to findings.8 The NIST Generative AI Profile recommends evaluating post-deployment monitoring. It also recommends comparing behavior with defined risk limits.9 Neither fixes detection rates, base rates, or thresholds for prompt injection, retrieval poisoning, or unusual tool use. Those stay deployment decisions with measured review.
Indicators can follow from the threat model, release tests, known faults or investigated incidents. For each indicator the design records the expected signal, threshold, required context, and response owner. A deployment still needs its own labeled outcomes and measurement population before it relies on an indicator’s precision. A forbidden-resource event counts as exact only when the resource identity and the policy version behind the decision are both resolved correctly. A resource spike needs a workload baseline to mean anything.

Example
Three causes for one spike. Suppose a worker’s accelerator use triples overnight against its baseline. The same signal fits a newly assigned batch workload, a runaway generation loop, and an attacker resubmitting expensive prompts. Reviewers check the job record, the submitting identity, and whether the prompts match assigned work before choosing among continued operation, a quota stop, or an incident declaration.
Conclusion. The spike alone selects no cause. The response team uses the job and identity records to choose a proportionate action. If those records do not distinguish the causes, the investigation remains open.

A detector with an enforcement connection allows ordinary processing, blocks a protected operation where it has that authority, and otherwise sends an alert. An advisory detector without such a connection can only report. A response team or another service must act on its alert. Its report keeps detected failures out of all confirmed failures beside valid alerts out of all alerts, with latency and review count alongside. Lower thresholds catch more variation at the price of interruptions and analyst work. Drift, sparse context, or activity kept below threshold can evade detection. Detector performance remains insufficient evidence that unobserved failures were absent.
crumbs: Part V: Testing controls and recovery

title: 15  Failures during live operation
text:
15.3 Changed controls and permissions
A system can drift out of its release record without any single dramatic event. Configuration edits, rotated or expired identities, swapped model versions, refreshed retrieval snapshots, and changed data permissions each alter one assumption the release evidence rested on.
The live check compares the active configuration against the release record. It checks which model version serves traffic, which retrieval snapshot answers queries, which tool schemas and permission policies apply, and which identities hold which rights. A mismatch does not prove harm. Reviewers identify which conclusions depend on the change, as in release decisions (Chapter 14). Suppose a retrieval snapshot gains documents from an additional source. Earlier tests limited to the old source set do not establish retrieval and permission behavior for the added documents. Tests of that new path can fill the missing coverage. Unrelated evidence does not need to be discarded merely because the snapshot changed.
Supplier-side changes need the same treatment with less direct control. A provider model update, permission change, or notice of new data handling reaches the organization as a supplier statement to be checked against the deployment’s assumptions. It is not an automatically accepted continuation. Rotation and expiry deserve their own watch. A rotation may allow old and new credentials to overlap for a specified period. Expiry validation may allow a defined clock tolerance. Monitoring compares acceptance with those actual rules and with the deployment’s revocation behavior. Acceptance beyond an enforced expiry or withdrawal deadline is a different result from acceptance during an allowed overlap.
Measurement for this check counts configurations that match the release record out of all sampled live configurations, with mismatches grouped by affected model, snapshot, schema, or permission. Drift checks cost verification work and can delay rollout when every mismatch demands review. A supplier notice can arrive late, be incomplete, or omit an effective date, which leaves the mismatch undetected until the next comparison. Findings feed recovery in Chapter 16, where the team restores a known good configuration or retests the affected path before resuming full operation.
crumbs: Part V: Testing controls and recovery

title: 15  Failures during live operation
text:
15.4 Missed failures and false alarms
Alert quality depends on detector performance and on how often the underlying event occurs. When true incidents are rare, even a sensitive detector can produce many false positives. Priority also weighs the protected asset, possible impact, confidence, and time available for containment. An alert without supporting context shifts reconstruction work onto the responder.
The NIST incident-response profile calls for detected events to be analyzed, correlated, placed in context, routed, and declared as incidents when criteria are met.10 It also calls for reports to be triaged, validated, categorized, and prioritized.11 The profile defines desired outcomes rather than an AI alert score or measured analyst workload. Precision and recall here keep the release-measurement meanings: real failures among alerts, and real failures caught among all real failures, as defined in release decisions (Chapter 14).

Example
Counting alerts when incidents are rare. Suppose one real incident hides among ten thousand routine events. A detector catches it but also flags ninety-nine ordinary events, producing one hundred alerts. Precision is 1 out of 100, or 1 percent. Observed recall is 1 out of 1. That single incident does not establish the detector’s sensitivity across a population.
Conclusion. The team has one hundred alerts to assess, of which ninety-nine concern routine events. Catching the incident does not establish that the resulting review workload is affordable. This sample illustrates why precision and review time matter alongside recall.

Each alert carries the trace identifier, triggering evidence, affected identity and asset, relevant control, severity basis, and responsible route. A grouping rule can combine repeated alerts about one event, but it needs a test for when events are actually the same. Grouping by a broad label can hide different affected users or targets. Investigation outcomes supply labels for later precision estimates and show how much review work each rule creates.
The routing service sets priority and destination from incident criteria, asset impact, confidence, and response ownership. Its denominator is every generated alert, with delivered, acknowledged, suppressed, escalated, and missed alerts counted separately. Faster escalation consumes analyst time and can interrupt low-risk work. Broad suppression, stale ownership, or unavailable communication can hide an urgent case. Delivery with acknowledgment does not prove correct triage.
crumbs: Part V: Testing controls and recovery

title: 15  Failures during live operation
text:
15.5 Failures of protective services
Detectors, policy services, log sinks, and reviewers can themselves slow down or go dark. Control resilience concerns the system’s behavior in exactly that state. A fail-open path continues the protected operation when its check fails or is unavailable. A fail-closed path blocks that operation under the same condition. The choice turns on the safety and availability consequences of each state. Quotas, rate limits, time limits, and stopping rules can remain enforceable even when a secondary detector fails.
Saltzer and Schroeder’s fail-safe-defaults principle bases access decisions on permission so that failure does not silently broaden access.12 The NIST Generative AI Profile recommends monitoring deployed models and judging performance against defined limits with organizational risk tolerance.13 Neither decides the fail state for every service. Neither tests degraded policy, logging, approval, and detector components.
In the reference design, the action service blocks consequential changes when current authorization is unavailable. It may serve a clearly marked read-only fallback from approved data only when it can still establish the reader’s current access and the data and release scope remain allowed. A fallback that cannot check access can disclose data the reader should no longer see. It buffers minimal local evidence under the same protections as the primary store until the protected log path returns, then applies the normal retention rule. A total outage can still lose whatever was never written.
Fault injection tests the enforcing service with unavailable policy, detector, log, approval, and identity dependencies. The report counts protected operations that entered the intended fail state out of all injected failures. It measures clean availability separately. That result covers the injected dependencies and operations only. Fail-open and fail-closed describe each specific protected operation under its failed check. Fail-closed behavior can stop legitimate work, while fail-open behavior accepts more security risk. A shared dependency failure or an untested fallback can defeat both paths. The correct fail state does not prove the retained evidence is complete.
crumbs: Part V: Testing controls and recovery

title: 15  Failures during live operation
text:
15.6 Operating limits and escalation
Thresholds only matter if crossing one changes what happens next. Error rates, cost movement, resource use, and unauthorized effects each get triggers agreed before deployment, drawn from the release thresholds and risk limits they monitor. The operating plan specifies the enforcing service, such as a scheduler that stops jobs exceeding a quota. It also assigns a response team and response time to alerts that need investigation.
Restriction narrows what the system may do: fewer permitted actions, tighter quotas, a smaller user or data scope. A pause stops the affected operation. Services that depend on the paused operation may also fail. The operating plan therefore identifies which essential functions can continue and which dependencies they still need. The read-only fallback continues only where its own access and scope checks still pass, not by default after every pause. The response team records the remaining risk of disruption and uses the joined records during recovery (Chapter 16). The responsible service owner decides whether operation resumes, resumes with restrictions, or remains stopped, using the recovery evidence. Spending and usage trends feed investment review in investment choices (Chapter 22).

Note
Chapter checkpoint. Suppose an application trace shows a normal answer with no approved tool action, while infrastructure records for the same request show denied external egress and a stopped process after the job exceeded its process limit. How should monitoring represent this event?
Answer. Join the application, scheduler, process, and network records with stable request and job identifiers. Preserve the model version, worker identity, destination, policy decisions, process counts, and final task state. Route an alert for unexpected egress plus resource-limit enforcement, with the joined records attached. The evidence supports a blocked abnormal path and an incomplete request. It does not establish attacker control or show that every route was observed.

title: 16  Recovering from AI incidents
text:
16.1 Incident triage
Security question. How does an organization contain an AI incident and know that recovery is complete?
Reference frame. Suppose responders have two incident packets. One contains document versions, identity decisions, tool requests, and incomplete supplier records. The other concerns a compromised organization-operated worker.
Investigation can start with an observed consequence or a warning of attempted harm, then work backward through identities, records, actions, and changed state. Recovery requires evidence that the identified failure path is blocked in the restored system.
A security event is an observable occurrence relevant to security. An incident is an event that meets the organization’s criteria for response. Triage separates ordinary model error from policy violation, hostile-content influence, account or infrastructure compromise, disclosure, and resource abuse. Classification matters because each path needs different evidence and containment.
NIST distinguishes cybersecurity events from incidents and places validation, categorization, prioritization, and incident declaration in the response process.1 It also presents response as part of continuing cybersecurity risk management rather than a separate linear phase.2 The profile does not supply AI-specific categories or one universal declaration threshold.
The hypothetical responder starts from a routed alert and checks the affected asset, observed outcome, identities, time window, system version, and supporting trace. A low-quality answer with no boundary violation remains a model-quality issue. A forbidden disclosure or unauthorized action enters incident handling. The declaration record states confidence and missing evidence. Preservation begins before containment changes volatile state.
The incident lead enforces triage by checking the event against documented criteria and affected assets. Observed outcomes and available evidence determine whether it is declared, downgraded, or escalated. The denominator is every routed event, with declarations, later reclassifications, and time to decision reported separately. Rapid triage consumes responder capacity and can interrupt service. Missing traces or an incorrect model-error label can hide an incident. Recovery reopens the case and preserves newly found evidence. Any containment change includes the reason for reclassification. A correct category does not prove complete scope.
crumbs: Part V: Testing controls and recovery

title: 16  Recovering from AI incidents
text:
16.2 Evidence preservation
Evidence preservation keeps records available and trustworthy enough to reconstruct the event. Relevant material can include prompts and outputs with retrieved document versions. Policy decisions, tool traces, model and code identities, process state, network events, credentials, and supplier records may also matter. Some data may already be missing or inaccessible, which belongs in the evidence record.
The NIST incident-response profile calls for recording response actions and preserving the integrity of incident records and data.3 NIST forensic guidance begins with identifying, labeling, recording, and acquiring relevant data while preserving integrity.4 The forensic publication predates current AI systems and does not supply an AI evidence list or legal procedure.
The responder copies volatile records first and records the acquisition time with its method. Stable files receive hashes. Access is restricted while original versions are preserved. Provider records are requested through the available contract, while unavailable fields remain explicit. Hashes can reveal later file changes but cannot prove that the original record was complete or truthful. Preserved artifacts provide the basis for timeline and scope analysis.

Example
Concrete preservation record (hypothetical). The operating mode is incident response to request req-882, which attempted an unapproved external connection. The preservation task starts before the worker is terminated because process and memory state are volatile.




Table 16.1: Evidence preservation sequence.











Order

2

3

4

For each stable export, the evidence register identifies the collector, time, method, access restriction, and file hash. It marks the provider trace as missing rather than treating silence as proof that no provider event occurred. The conclusion is that the listed artifacts can support a bounded timeline and integrity check. The shortened identifiers and results are hypothetical, and hashes cannot show that the original logs were complete.
An incident responder preserves evidence only after checking each expected source, acquisition method, time, integrity record, access rule, and storage result. The coverage denominator is all sources required by the incident map, with acquired, unavailable, overwritten, and untrusted items separated. Preservation costs storage and can retain sensitive content longer than ordinary operations allow. Volatile loss, tampered source logs, or inaccessible supplier records can bypass the record. Recovery captures later snapshots and requests external evidence. Weak artifacts receive restricted use when conclusions are updated. A matching hash proves only that the captured file did not later change.
crumbs: Part V: Testing controls and recovery

title: 16  Recovering from AI incidents
text:
16.3 Incident investigation and scope
Investigation links the initial entry point to affected identities and accessed records. It then checks executed actions and modified artifacts. Observed harm is recorded separately. A timeline orders evidence from application, identity, retrieval, tool, provider, host, and network sources. Competing explanations remain under consideration until the records distinguish them. Attribution confidence remains separate from confidence about the technical path.
NIST forensic guidance separates collection, examination, analysis, and reporting across files, operating systems, networks, and application data.5 The NIST incident-response profile includes root-cause analysis as a response outcome.6 These sources provide process structure without making attribution certain or defining AI-specific artifacts.
In the hypothetical case, the team correlates a hostile document version with its retrieval, the model request, a proposed tool call, the policy decision, and the external result. It checks whether account compromise or a changed tool service could produce the same trace. Each conclusion cites supporting and conflicting records. The scoped identities, components, sources, and destinations define the containment set. Persistence adds a further check because some AI effects remain after removal of the initial trigger. Poisoned model weights, a contaminated retrieval index, copies in caches and agent memory, altered configuration or code, and exposed credentials each require a different recovery path and leave different evidence. The investigation therefore tags each affected asset with its persistence type and the remaining spread.
The case lead accepts or rejects each path hypothesis after checking its required events against the preserved timeline. The denominator is every system, identity, record, and destination reachable from the supported path, with examined and unresolved items reported separately. Wider scope consumes time and delays restoration. Missing telemetry, false correlation, or a second entry point can leave the scope too small. Recovery expands containment and collects new sources. The revised timeline then supports another review of affected conclusions. A coherent path does not establish actor attribution or exclude concurrent activity.
crumbs: Part V: Testing controls and recovery

title: 16  Recovering from AI incidents
text:
16.4 Incident containment
Containment reduces ongoing harm while preserving enough state for investigation. Available actions include revoking credentials and suspending a tool. The organization can also isolate a worker or block a destination. Freezing an affected data source and narrowing user access address other paths. The sequence depends on which path is active and whether a change would destroy volatile evidence.
The NIST incident-response profile calls for incidents to be contained and eradicated.7 International secure AI guidance recommends preparing incident procedures and mechanisms for responsible deployment and operation.8 These outcome statements do not choose the right containment action or sequence for the current incident.
For the hostile-document case, the organization first preserves the source and traces, then disables the affected connector and action credential. If a worker compromise remains possible, it isolates that workload and blocks external routes. Each containment action has an owner, expected effect, validation check, and reversal condition. Once the path is stable, recovery can restore known assets and permissions.

Example
Containment sequence for req-882 (hypothetical). Suppose triage confirms a retrieval poison path with attempted egress. The responder first records volatile process state, then revokes the action credential cred-A, disables connector conn-RAG-02, isolates worker job-417, and blocks destination 203.0.113.44 at the gateway. Each step records owner, time, and validation such as denied tool call or blocked connection attempt. Volatile capture precedes isolation so that stopping the worker does not erase the open-connection evidence.
Conclusion. The five actions together block the known retrieval and egress paths for that identity and workload. An alternate destination or a second compromised credential would remain outside this contained set and needs its own check.

The identity service and connector manager revoke access according to the supported path. Destination blocking occurs at the network gateway, while the workload controller isolates execution. The measure is confirmed blocked paths over all known active paths, with service impact and unresolved routes recorded beside it. Broad containment interrupts legitimate work and may destroy volatile state if applied too early. Unknown credentials, alternate connectors, or a compromised control plane can bypass local action. Recovery widens isolation and rotates related access. Affected control components are replaced before each path is validated again, while blocking known routes remains insufficient evidence that the incident has ended.
crumbs: Part V: Testing controls and recovery

title: 16  Recovering from AI incidents
text:
16.5 Recovery verification
Recovery restores a known state and demonstrates that the incident path no longer works. Affected state may include application code and model packages. System prompts, indexes, caches, agent memory, credentials, tool schemas, and access policy may also require restoration. Service availability alone cannot establish recovery if the same disclosure or action remains possible.
The NIST incident-response profile calls for checking restoration assets before use and verifying restored systems. It also calls for confirmation of normal operation before recovery is declared complete.9 The NIST Generative AI Profile recommends post-incident review and practice of response plans.10 These sources leave AI-specific checks for indexes, caches, memory, and authorization to the recovery design.
The hypothetical recovery rebuilds the index from approved source versions and clears affected caches. It rotates credentials before restoring reviewed configuration and rerunning the original failure trace. It also runs clean task cases to confirm that the service still works. Each affected asset has a test and expected result. Passing those tests supports a bounded recovery decision and provides evidence for follow-up actions.

Example
Retest before return to service (hypothetical). Suppose the team restores eight assets for req-882 including source index, cache, and policy snapshot. It reruns the original hostile-document trace and expects a blocked or safe response, and it runs twelve clean tasks that should still succeed. If the hostile trace is blocked and ten clean tasks pass while two fail for an unrelated permission error, recovery has blocked the failure path but introduced a separate availability issue. If the hostile trace still triggers egress, restoration is incomplete even when the dashboard shows service as up.
Conclusion. Return to service is supported only when the original failure trace is blocked and intended work still succeeds on the restored assets. Partial clean-task failure requires a separate fix and a new retest.

The recovery owner authorizes return to service only after checking every affected asset, original failure case, clean task, identity, destination, and remaining evidence gap. The denominator is all required recovery checks, with pass, fail, blocked, and unavailable results kept separate. Rebuilds and repeated tests extend downtime and can lose useful cached state. An untracked copy, unchanged supplier component, or weak regression case can preserve the failure. Another failed check rolls back the attempted restoration and narrows service. The missing state is corrected before the gate runs again. Passing supports the tested state only.
crumbs: Part V: Testing controls and recovery

title: 16  Recovering from AI incidents
text:
16.6 Post incident improvement
Follow-up turns incident evidence into changes to controls, tests, contracts, and training. It also decides which records remain for legal, operational, or research purposes and which data and access must be removed. Service retirement includes revoking identities and disabling connectors. It also ends supplier access and checks known derived stores.
The NIST incident-response profile integrates lessons and improvement into risk management after response and recovery.11 NIST media-sanitization guidance separates the sanitization decision from verification and validation of the result.12 Media sanitization alone cannot prove deletion from hosted-model parameters, supplier backups, indexes, or distributed caches.
The organization assigns each corrective action to a responsible owner and links it to a test or contract result. Retention and notification follow current sector and jurisdiction rules, which require separate legal sources. Supplier exit evidence records what the organization can verify and what remains outside its visibility. The incident record also shows why harmful activity does not by itself prove that AI caused or improved it. Chapter 17 changes the object of analysis from an AI system under attack to an attacker using AI, then applies the same separation of observation, inference, and unsupported attribution.
The closure owner chooses retention, deletion, retirement, or reopening after checking corrective-action evidence, access revocation, supplier response, and applicable obligations. The denominator is every agreed follow-up action and every service identity or connector in the retirement record. Longer retention raises storage and privacy cost, while early deletion can weaken later investigation. An unlisted supplier copy or forgotten credential can bypass retirement. Recovery extends the hold when justified and revokes remaining access. Missing evidence is requested before closure checks run again because administrative closure does not prove deletion from systems outside organizational visibility.

Note
Chapter checkpoint. A hostile document influenced request req-882, which then attempted external egress. The worker was stopped, but the provider trace is unavailable. What response record supports containment and recovery?
Answer. Preserve volatile process and connection state first, followed by application, retrieval, policy, tool, runtime, identity, and network records. Record acquisition details, hashes for stable exports, access limits, and the missing provider evidence. Use the available path evidence to guide credential revocation and worker isolation. Urgent containment need not wait for a complete reconstruction. Rebuild the index from approved document versions, clear affected caches, rotate exposed credentials, and rerun the original failure trace plus clean tasks. Recovery is supported only when the prohibited path fails and intended work still succeeds. Missing provider evidence remains a limit on scope and attribution.

Supplier evidence, logical deletion, and jurisdiction-specific notification duties still require case-specific review.

Starter literature. These sources provide the initial evidence base for the chapter and guide later research, but they do not support every claim by themselves. 13 14

title: Part VI: Assessing AI in cybersecurity
text:
Chapters in this part
Claims about AI in cybersecurity require separate evidence for attacker assistance, defensive value, and deployment cost.
The same security task is examined from three sides: how AI changes harmful work, how an assistant changes defensive work, and which model and hosting arrangement can deliver the measured benefit within the required permissions and operating budget.
crumbs: Part VI: Assessing AI in cybersecurity

title: Part VI: Assessing AI in cybersecurity
text:
AI’s role in harmful activity: An evidence ladder separates demonstrated capability, observed AI-assisted harm, prevalence, and the controls justified by each level.
AI in defensive work: A defensive AI assessment measures useful security work while keeping human judgment, data access, and action authority visible.
Choosing a viable deployment: A deployment comparison fixes task, data access, quality target, action limits, and full operating cost before comparing external, managed, and internal models.
crumbs: Part VI: Assessing AI in cybersecurity

title: 17  AI’s role in harmful activity
text:
17.1 AI across attack workflows
Security question. Which parts of an attack can AI improve, and what evidence shows that the improvement matters?
Reference frame. The analysis now concerns an attacker using AI assistance against an organization. It keeps hypothetical impersonation examples separate from identified incident or laboratory evidence because generated content alone does not show autonomous operation. Chapter 13 supplies the action-sequence context and Chapter 14 supplies the evaluation methods used to judge each claim.
The same threat and evaluation discipline applies when AI assists an attacker. Capability demonstrations, observed use, prevalence, and measured effect support different conclusions, and each requires its own evidence.
Finding AI somewhere in an intrusion does not show that it changed the attack. Assessment starts by locating its role in reconnaissance, vulnerability work, social engineering, code generation, operations, or analysis of stolen data. The evidence then distinguishes simple assistance from higher speed, scale, quality, success, or a capability that was otherwise unavailable.
The UK National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) places current AI use across several intrusion activities in its highest likelihood band. The activities include reconnaissance, exploit development, social engineering, basic malware generation, and processing of exfiltrated data.1 It expects near-term growth mainly through existing tactics, techniques, and procedures.2 This probabilistic intelligence assessment covers the period through 2027 without supplying a controlled experiment or incident count.
For each claim, the organization records the task, model access, human input, tools, baseline, output, and observed operational result. “AI assisted reconnaissance” is weaker than evidence that it found more valid targets in less time under the same conditions. This common evidence frame supports the impersonation, programming, automation, and incident examples that follow.
The records show model assistance during information synthesis and human control over selection and sending. They do not show faster discovery or more valid contacts. They also leave autonomous operation and any new capability unsupported. The conclusion is limited to observed assistance in one stage. Every role and record in this assessment is hypothetical.
The reviewer accepts a capability statement only after checking the task, model access, human steps, baseline, measured result, and missing records. The denominator is every assessed intrusion stage, with supported, unsupported, and unknown AI effects kept separate. Detailed review takes analyst time and depends on access to sensitive records. Incomplete reporting or selection of only successful episodes can bypass the comparison. Recovery narrows or withdraws the claim while missing evidence is requested. The assessment then runs again, but an accepted role claim still does not establish improvement or prevalence.
crumbs: Part VI: Assessing AI in cybersecurity
17  AI's role in harmful activity

title: 17  AI’s role in harmful activity
text:
Example
Concrete role assessment (hypothetical). The operating mode is retrospective review of an intrusion report. The reported task was finding public employee contact details. The actor supplied search terms to an external model and manually selected results. An ordinary mailing tool then sent the messages. The report contains model transcripts and sent-message records but no comparison with unaided research.
crumbs: Part VI: Assessing AI in cybersecurity
17  AI's role in harmful activity

title: 17  AI’s role in harmful activity
text:
17.2 Impersonation and fraud
Impersonation combines a false identity claim with a business process that accepts the claim. Generated text, voice, image, or video can increase realism or scale. The consequential failure occurs when a person or system authorizes a payment. Sharing sensitive data or changing access are other possible effects. Assessment keeps the synthetic content and the transaction path separate.
The FBI reported a campaign beginning in April 2025 that used text messages and AI-generated voice messages while impersonating senior United States officials.3 The agency recommends independent verification through a known contact method instead of relying on the received message.4 The alert documents one campaign and advice. It does not estimate prevalence or measure a verification control’s effectiveness.
In a hypothetical finance case, a synthetic voice instructs an employee to change a supplier account. The defensive trace records the claimed identity and received channel. It then records the requested transaction, independent callback, and authorization result. Even perfect media detection would leave the business process exposed to ordinary impersonation. This example shows why the AI claim and the process failure need separate evidence.
The transaction service enforces the decision by checking the account, requested change, independent verification result, current approver, and second approval where required. The test reports blocked impersonation attempts over all eligible attempts and legitimate changes delayed or rejected over all valid requests. Independent contact adds time and can slow urgent work. Compromise of the verification channel or collusion can bypass it. Recovery freezes the change and reverses the transaction when possible. Affected access is reset before verification runs again, although one blocked attempt does not measure general effectiveness or prove that the content was synthetic.
crumbs: Part VI: Assessing AI in cybersecurity
17  AI's role in harmful activity

title: 17  AI’s role in harmful activity
text:
17.3 Technical assistance measurement
Programming and analysis assistance can help with code generation, translation, debugging, vulnerability research, exploit work, and interpretation of large data sets. A capability claim needs a defined task and a baseline with comparable access, time, skill, and success criteria. Output volume alone does not establish useful attacker progress.
The NCSC assessment includes vulnerability research, exploit development, basic malware generation, and data processing among activities that AI can assist.5 Pearce and colleagues found vulnerable suggestions in some scenarios tested with an early GitHub Copilot version.6 The first source lacks controlled task baselines, while the second studied defensive code quality rather than attacker productivity.
A useful experiment compares people with and without the assistant on the same eligible tasks under the same model access, skill, time, tools, and success rules, then measures valid findings, time, false claims, required correction, and end-to-end success. Current packet sources do not provide that controlled attacker-uplift result, so the magnitude remains unknown. Clear task evidence is also needed before describing the work as automated.

Example
Worked evidence assessment (hypothetical). The operating mode is a controlled comparison on eight synthetic code-analysis tasks. The same four participants alternate between unaided work and an assistant. The target for each task is a previously planted defect with a fixed validation test.

The observed intermediate results show one additional valid finding and 18 fewer elapsed minutes with the assistant, alongside two additional false claims and 11 additional correction minutes. The conclusion is that assistance changed outcomes in this small exercise under these access conditions. It does not establish attacker productivity in operational systems because the sample is small, task order may matter, and the participants and synthetic defects may not represent real attacks. All values are hypothetical.
The reviewer accepts an uplift claim only when the baseline and assistant conditions use the same eligible tasks, access, validation tests, and outcome rules. The denominator is all assigned tasks and participants, with valid findings, false claims, elapsed time, and correction time reported separately. Controlled comparison consumes expert time and can reveal sensitive techniques. Learning effects, task mismatch, or selective reporting can bypass the inference. Recovery withdraws the claim and corrects the design before the comparison runs again. A measured difference does not establish operational harm.

title: 17  AI’s role in harmful activity
text:
17.4 Degrees of automation
Automation has observable steps. A person may request and select each output. A fixed script may repeat preset operations, while a model may choose a sequence. A tool loop may change that sequence after observing results. Claims of autonomy become specific only when they identify who sets the goal and chooses actions. They also identify who supplies credentials and reviews results. The stopping authority is recorded separately.
MITRE ATLAS labels technique evidence as Feasible, Demonstrated, or Realized.7 The NCSC assessment distinguishes AI assistance across intrusion stages but does not define a general automation scale.8 ATLAS maturity concerns evidence for a technique rather than the level of agent control. These sources do not support a precise universal autonomy taxonomy.
The descriptive trace uses separate records for human selection and fixed automation. Model planning, tool execution, and adaptation also receive separate records. A system can plan without permission to act, or execute a fixed script without model planning. The cited sources do not establish one operational scale. This trace lets benchmark and incident reports state exactly what occurred.
The claim reviewer allows an automation label only after checking who set the goal and selected actions. The review also checks who supplied credentials and approved effects. It records who observed results and stopped the sequence. The denominator is every consequential step in the reported workflow, with human, fixed-software, model-selected, and unknown control recorded separately. Detailed tracing costs storage and investigative time. Missing tool logs or hidden human intervention can bypass the classification. Recovery lowers the claim to the strongest supported level and seeks the absent records. A complete step trace does not establish greater capability or success.

title: 17  AI’s role in harmful activity
text:
17.5 Incident and benchmark evidence
Security sources answer different questions. Feasibility means a mechanism can work under stated conditions. A controlled demonstration shows it in an experiment. An observed incident records operational use. Prevalence estimates how often it occurs in a defined population. Attribution links activity to an actor or system with stated confidence. Moving up this ladder requires new evidence.
MITRE ATLAS separates Feasible, Demonstrated, and Realized technique maturity.9 The NCSC report states assessed likelihoods and a forecast horizon, while the FBI alert records a specific campaign.10 The FBI case supports observed AI-assisted impersonation without establishing frequency.11 Combining an intelligence assessment and one alert cannot create a prevalence estimate.
An evidence record captures source type, access and task conditions, model or tool version, baseline, observed result, reporting incentives, and uncertainty. A vendor demonstration may establish feasibility. A first-party incident report may establish observed use but still omit attribution detail. This ladder prevents a laboratory result from becoming a claim about common operational harm and sets the standard for information-manipulation claims.
The reviewer assigns the strongest supported class only after checking all required fields and the source’s direct observations. The denominator is every report assessed for the claim in the defined population, with accepted, rejected, duplicate, and incomplete sources separated and collection methods recorded. Collection and verification consume analyst time, while strict admission can leave timely questions unresolved. Publication bias, missing incidents, unknown cases, or copied reporting can distort the evidence set. Recovery changes the label and retracts unsupported synthesis. After the corpus is refreshed, several accepted incidents still do not create a prevalence estimate without a defined population and denominator.

title: 17  AI’s role in harmful activity
text:
17.6 Information manipulation paths
Information manipulation involves more than producing synthetic content. A complete claim connects content generation, coordinated distribution, audience exposure, measured effect, and attribution. Evidence for one link cannot silently stand for the others. Source verification also differs from judging whether the content changed beliefs or behavior.
The NCSC cyber-threat assessment explicitly excludes influence operations from its scope.12 MITRE ATLAS can organize technique and case evidence but cannot establish audience effect or campaign attribution by itself.13 These limits mean that neither source supports a prevalence or behavioral-effect claim about information manipulation.
The organization records each link as supported, disputed, or unknown and keeps platform observations separate from claims about human effect. Synthetic content may be confirmed while coordination and attribution remain uncertain.
Content authentication binds statements about a file’s origin or edit history to the file so that a validator can check them. C2PA Content Credentials use signed claims and content bindings for this purpose.14 They can support a statement about the signer and recorded history, but they can be absent or removed and do not establish that the depicted event is true. Statistical watermarking changes a generator’s output distribution so a detector can test for a hidden signal. Kirchenbauer and colleagues demonstrated one language-model method and measured its detection and quality tradeoffs.15 Detection depends on the scheme, text length, model access, and later editing. A watermark result supplies one signal rather than identity, intent, distribution, or audience effect.
Reputable research that measures generation, distribution, exposure, effect, and attribution is still required. Defensive priorities can proceed from verified failure paths without waiting for every broader campaign claim.
The reviewer accepts a campaign-effect claim only when evidence covers content, distribution, audience exposure, measured response, and attribution under stated criteria. The denominator must be the defined exposed population rather than the number of collected posts. Such measurement is costly, raises privacy concerns, and often arrives after the response decision. Activity outside the platform, weak sampling, or correlated reporting can bypass the study. Recovery narrows or withdraws the claim and updates controls from the links that remain supported. This correction still treats verified synthetic content as insufficient proof of coordination or behavioral effect.

title: 17  AI’s role in harmful activity
text:
17.7 Responses to AI assisted abuse
A defensive response targets the verified path by which harm occurs. Identity and transaction verification can reduce impersonation risk without identifying whether media was generated. Rate limits, reporting channels, account controls, and detection rules address other observed steps. The response record links each control to the evidence and outcome it is expected to change.
The FBI recommends verifying identity through an independently identified contact method and confirming requests for money or sensitive information before acting.16 The NCSC expects much near-term AI impact to use existing intrusion methods.17 Applying controls to those existing paths follows from that assessment. It does not compare the measured performance of defensive products.
In the hypothetical supplier-change process, an independent callback and second transaction approval protect the change even when content detection is uncertain. The organization records attempted bypasses, false positives, response time, and confirmed outcomes. New evidence can change control priority without changing the basic asset and authorization analysis. The same evidence discipline next tests an AI assistant used by the defensive team.
The identity and transaction services enforce the callback and approval rules from the trusted contact record, requested change, current account state, and approver identities. The evaluation reports harmful changes prevented over all confirmed attempts and legitimate changes delayed or denied over all valid requests. Added verification increases workload and transaction time. A compromised contact record, insider collusion, or recovery process with weaker checks can bypass it. Recovery freezes affected accounts and reverses supported changes. Verification channels are reset before the route is reviewed. Passing does not measure media detection or stop abuse through a different business process.

Note
Chapter checkpoint. A report states that an attacker “used AI autonomously” in a fraud attempt. The available records show that a person prompted a model and selected one generated message. The person sent it through an ordinary account, and the attempt failed when the employee used an independent callback. What can the organization conclude?
Answer. Human-directed generation assistance and the observed impersonation attempt are the strongest supported claims. Model-selected goals and tool execution remain unsupported. Prevalence and improvement against an unaided baseline remain unmeasured. The failed transaction shows that the independent callback protected this case, while one case cannot measure the control’s general effectiveness. The assessment should preserve those supported and unsupported claims separately.

Available sources still leave attacker productivity, automation levels, influence effects, and defensive effectiveness uncertain.

Starter literature. These sources provide the initial evidence base for the chapter and guide later research, but they do not support every claim by themselves. 18 19

title: 18  AI in defensive work
text:
18.1 AI supported alert triage
Security question. When does AI improve security work without creating unacceptable new errors or access?
Reference frame. Suppose a defensive analyst assistant reads synthetic alerts and intelligence documents through an external model and retrieval application. The model proposes responses, and a connected service checks permissions and required approvals before executing an action.
AI can also assist defensive work, but a useful summary is not a security decision. The analyst keeps judgment over priority and next steps, while a separate service controls action authority. Evaluation must include source support, correction effort, unauthorized effects, and analyst time before any claim of defensive value.
An AI assistant can help an analyst connect related events and draft an alert summary, but the summary must preserve the evidence needed to check it. Inputs include normalized events, identity and asset context, prior activity, and the rule that produced the alert. Evaluation counts missed incidents, unsupported statements, correction work, and analyst time as well as apparent speed.
The NIST incident-response profile calls for analysis and correlation of detected events before responders place them in context and route them.1 It also calls for validation and categorization of reports before prioritization and response.2 The profile does not evaluate AI summaries or define how they should express uncertainty.
In the hypothetical workflow, the assistant links each summary sentence to event identifiers and marks missing context. The analyst can inspect the source events before accepting a priority or incident declaration. A baseline compares the same alert set without the assistant. The sources cited here do not establish field performance for AI-assisted triage quality, time, correction, and missed incidents. The evidence-display rule carries into investigation and threat intelligence.
Control review. The triage application checks whether each summary statement includes an event identifier and whether the analyst accepted the priority. It withholds an incident declaration when either check fails. The test reports unsupported statements and missed incidents over all alerts in the fixed set, together with analyst minutes per accepted alert. Source linking and review add latency. They can still fail when the event store is incomplete or the analyst accepts a weak summary. Recovery returns the alert to the ordinary queue and preserves the draft, correction, and source events. This evidence supports the tested alert population only.
crumbs: Part VI: Assessing AI in cybersecurity

title: 18  AI in defensive work
text:
18.2 AI supported investigations
Investigation moves from observations to explanations. An observation records something seen. An indicator describes a pattern that may support detection or assessment. The assistant can retrieve reports and connect objects, but it must preserve external references, versions, confidence, and competing explanations so that the analyst can inspect the basis of a conclusion.
Structured Threat Information Expression (STIX) 2.1 separates observations, indicators, relationships, external references, confidence, and object versions in a structured threat-intelligence model.3 STIX also defines confidence as a common property and specifies mappings to other confidence scales.4 The schema can carry evidence and confidence. It cannot make the assistant’s inference correct.
The hypothetical assistant produces a claim, supporting observation identifiers, external references, confidence method, and at least one plausible alternative when the evidence permits. A confidence number without a method remains a label. Version links show when a report changed. This source-linked record supports later vulnerability and development decisions without hiding uncertainty.
Control review. The investigation workspace checks for a source identifier, source version, confidence method, and review status before a claim enters a case record. It accepts, returns, or marks the claim unresolved. A test counts complete claim records over all assistant claims and separately counts accepted claims later corrected. The check costs analyst time and storage. Copied text that enters another system without its record can bypass the check, while even an attached record does not establish a claim as true. Recovery withdraws the claim and restores the earlier case state. Affected analysts receive an alert.
crumbs: Part VI: Assessing AI in cybersecurity

title: 18  AI in defensive work
text:
18.3 AI supported development
For vulnerability and development work, the assistant may explain a finding or inspect dependency data. It may also draft a patch or propose a test. The security decision still depends on the real code, build, deployment conditions, and authorization for testing. A generated fix needs review and execution evidence rather than acceptance based on a plausible explanation.
The NIST Secure Software Development Framework calls for verification of third-party components, code review, executable-code testing, and triage of results.5 Pearce and colleagues found vulnerable suggestions in some scenarios tested with an early GitHub Copilot version.6 That finding does not transfer automatically to later models or workflows with independent review.
The organization links the assistant’s recommendation to the finding, dependency identity, generated diff, authorized test environment, test output, reviewer, and deployment result. Production testing requires separate permission. A rejected suggestion remains part of evaluation evidence because it contributes to correction cost. These records separate recommendation quality from the authority to act.
Control review. The change pipeline checks the finding identifier, repository revision, test-environment authorization, reviewer decision, and required test result before allowing a merge or deployment. It blocks incomplete or failed candidates. Evaluation reports accepted fixes, rejected fixes, and later regressions over all submitted suggestions, plus review minutes per accepted fix. The gate delays delivery and can miss a defect outside the test set. Because the gate covers only the tested deployment conditions, recovery reverts to the recorded accepted revision and revokes temporary test access.

title: 18  AI in defensive work
text:
18.4 Human and automated roles
The assistant’s role can range from summary to constrained execution. A suggested action tells the analyst what could be done. A drafted action prepares exact arguments for review. Constrained execution runs only an authorized operation within fixed limits. Escalation transfers the decision and evidence to a person or service with the required authority.
Least privilege and complete mediation support granting only task-specific rights and checking access when the protected object is used.7 MCP recommends making exposed tools visible to users and preserving their ability to deny an invocation.8 These principles do not identify the best division of labor or measure the quality of human approval.
The hypothetical assistant may query read-only telemetry and draft a host-isolation request. A separate service resolves the host and checks policy. Before execution, it displays the host, operation, and effect, and records analyst approval, keeping judgment and authority visible. Recovery tests cover an incorrect recommendation and a partial action. The sources cited here do not supply controlled comparisons of analyst-only, assistant-only, and combined workflows. This authority map defines what an attacker could misuse.
Control review. The action service enforces the boundary by checking the analyst identity, target host, requested operation, approval, and current incident state. It allows only the approved action or returns a denial. Tests count unauthorized and incorrectly completed actions over all attempted actions, including partial failures. Approval adds delay, while constrained execution adds engineering and support cost. A stale approval or alternate management interface can bypass the intended path. The test does not measure whether the recommendation itself was correct. Recovery cancels pending work and restores the host where possible, while irreversible effects receive escalation.

title: 18  AI in defensive work
text:
18.5 Attacks on defensive assistants
A defensive assistant consumes attacker-influenced material by design. Logs, tickets, repositories, malware reports, and intelligence documents can contain instructions or data crafted to influence its output. The resulting risk depends on sensitive telemetry, retrieval access, tool permissions, and retained memory available to the assistant.
Greshake and colleagues demonstrated indirect prompt injection through external content and effects on connected actions in selected systems.9 OWASP’s 2026 description includes tool output, retrieved content, and persistent memory as prompt-injection paths and links impact to available functions and permissions.10 The research demonstrations establish selected attack paths, while OWASP categorizes risks and recommends mitigations. Neither source proves that a current security assistant is vulnerable or that a proposed control works.
A hypothetical test places a hostile instruction in a synthetic ticket that the assistant must summarize. The trace follows retrieval, context, response, proposed tools, and policy decisions. The expected result is an evidence-linked summary with no unauthorized query or action. This test counts failures alongside useful work when the organization measures operational value.
Control review. The retrieval application limits eligible records, and the action service checks every proposed operation independently of model text. The test denominator is all hostile tickets replayed under the specified identities and permissions. It reports summaries changed by hostile text, restricted records returned, and actions allowed. Filtering and independent authorization consume compute and review time. Encoded instructions, a compromised connector, or an unmediated tool path can defeat parts of the design. Recovery removes the ticket from active context and revokes affected credentials. It then restores the accepted configuration and retests the same cases. A clean run does not cover unseen instruction forms.
crumbs: Part VI: Assessing AI in cybersecurity

title: 18  AI in defensive work
text:
18.6 Operational value
Operational value is the measured benefit of the assistant after errors, correction work, review, security controls, privacy effects, and total operating cost are included. A fair comparison uses the same alert or investigation workload and a human or deterministic baseline. Quality measures depend on the decision, such as correct triage, supported findings, or safe completion.
The AI RMF MEASURE function calls for documented methods, metrics, test sets, limitations, human review, and monitoring.11 NIST AI 800-3 says the evaluation target should match the decision and separates item variation from repeated-trial variation.12 The publications do not supply an operational-value result for a security assistant.
The organization reports how often the task succeeds, how much analyst time and correction it requires, which incidents are missed, which consequential errors remain, and what the system and its review cost. Sampling and uncertainty belong in the same report because faster summaries do not justify deployment when they hide missed incidents or create unsafe actions. A strong field study that combines these measures is still needed. Chapter 19 uses this measured task and boundary to compare deployment options.
Operating fallback. The service owner operates a deterministic severity queue and documents an analyst-only path for the same alert population. During a continuity test, the record shows alerts processed through each fallback over all alerts received during the outage, time to first usable result, and unresolved backlog at restoration. Maintaining parallel rules and analyst capacity raises ongoing cost. A fallback can fail when source systems are unavailable or staff capacity is exhausted. Because one exercise does not establish capacity for a longer or broader disruption, recovery returns work in priority order and reconciles duplicate decisions.
Controlled comparison. This hypothetical evaluation runs in evaluation mode. It does not update model parameters or permit an external action. The task is to prioritize 120 synthetic alerts drawn from 12 incident stories. Senior analysts establish the reference priority and supporting event identifiers before the comparison. Each method receives the same alerts, identity context, time limit, and read-only access.

All values are exercise values, not measured findings. The intermediate record for the combined method contains the assistant summary, cited event identifiers, analyst correction, and final priority. In this example, the combined method saves 120 analyst minutes compared with the analyst-only method and has one fewer consequential error. The fourteen corrected drafts show why accepted output alone is an incomplete measure. The result supports a limited pilot under the tested read-only conditions. It does not support autonomous response or transfer to a different alert population.

Note
Chapter checkpoint. Does the lower analyst time for the combined method justify giving the assistant permission to isolate hosts?
Answer. No. The evaluation measured read-only triage under analyst control. Host isolation changes external state and can interrupt service. That operating mode needs a separate authorization path, action tests, recovery tests, and evidence about harmful interventions. The comparison supports only the task and permissions that were tested.

Triage outcomes, the division of work between analyst and assistant, and full operating cost still need stronger operational evidence.

title: 19  Choosing a viable deployment
text:
19.1 Deployment rights and duties
Security question. Which combination of model, hosting, and controls fits a specified security task?
Reference frame. Suppose the same defensive task and organization workload are run under three explicitly described arrangements: an external model API operated by a supplier, a managed platform that runs an organization-controlled model on rented infrastructure, and an internal deployment that runs the same model on the organization’s own infrastructure. Task inputs, expected results, allowed actions, data access, quality target, and oversight requirements remain constant where possible so that differences in behavior, evidence, and cost reflect the deployment and not the task.
An external service, a managed platform, and an internal model can each support the same defensive task. The comparison uses the same task, permissions, workload, quality target, and adversarial conditions while examining rights, duties, and full operating cost.
A deployment label leaves inspection rights and operating duties unclear. A hosted model service provides model access through a supplier-operated interface. A self-hosted model deployment runs model software that loads specified weights on infrastructure operated or controlled by the adopting organization. A managed platform is the third case: the organization operates the model but the supplier operates the underlying hosts, networks, and patching of that platform. Access to the weights, license rights, runtime control, dependencies, and update duties remain separate facts in all three arrangements.
Modification rights are permissions granted by a license or contract to alter and reuse supplied material. The Open Source Initiative definition goes further than access to model weights: it requires freedom to use, study, modify, and share an AI system, together with access to the preferred form for modification.1 This definition does not classify every downloadable model or settle how a license applies in a license dispute.
Security also depends on the operator who patches the runtime and controls the network, including who can observe prompts, retrieved context, model outputs, logs, and credentials. Identity, isolation, logging, incident response, and access to evidence follow the same operator boundary, as described in Chapter 7, Chapter 8, and Chapter 9. International secure-design guidance treats model choice as a comparison across security, privacy, performance, and transparency, without ranking one hosting arrangement as generally best.2 These rights and duties define the feasible choices for the intervention comparison that follows, before quality or cost decides the outcome.
Rights trace. The hypothetical organization compares the three arrangements for the fixed alert triage task introduced in Chapter 18. The input is redacted alert text, the target is a cited priority recommendation, and neither option may execute a response. The external service contract permits use through its interface but does not provide model weights and retains runtime patching and network control. The managed option permits organization control of the model while the supplier retains host patching and physical control. The internal option permits local runtime inspection and modification under its selected license, while the organization assumes patching, network, and recovery duties. The observed result is a deployment record with four field pairs: operating control and access to weights, followed by modification rights and update responsibility. The conclusion is that the words external, managed, and internal do not answer those four questions without the record.
Decision control. Architecture reviewers check those four fields, the allowed data, the permitted model and platform operators, and the recovery duty before approving any option. They postpone the choice when a required right or operator is missing. The review reports complete deployment records over all candidates and the annual labor required to maintain each accepted option. Contract ambiguity and undocumented subcontracting can defeat the check. Recovery uses the tested alternate service or manual path while the organization resolves the missing right. A complete record does not prove that the supplier or internal operator will meet the stated duty.

title: 19  Choosing a viable deployment
text:
19.2 Selecting the smallest intervention
The deployment decision becomes confused when the organization treats every missing capability as a reason to train a model. The useful question is what is missing. Prompting supplies task instructions with a request. Retrieval adds selected external material to the current context. Tool access allows the application to call another function or service. Fine-tuning changes model parameters through further training on task data.
NIST’s generative AI profile says that intended-purpose analysis includes internal or external use, narrow or broad scope, fine-tuning, and retrieval-based data sources.3 The list identifies factors to examine but does not establish the right intervention for a task. The packet lacks a controlled study comparing all four choices under the same task, model, data, and evaluation conditions.
The mechanism determines the security work. Retrieval adds source eligibility and instruction-data confusion. Tool access adds identity and action authorization. Fine-tuning adds training data, versioned parameters, and regression testing. A conservative design uses the smallest change that addresses the observed gap, then treats that choice as a hypothesis to test under the same task, permissions, and quality target that later deployments will use. The selected intervention determines the evidence and recovery material in the adaptation workflow.
Decision control. Change reviewers record the observed gap and check whether prompting, retrieval, a tool, or fine-tuning changes data access, parameters, or action authority. They allow a pilot only when the selected change has a matching test and rollback point. Results report accepted task cases and security failures over all pilot cases. More capable interventions increase integration, review, and recovery work. The rule can fail when the original gap is measured poorly or several changes are bundled. Recovery disables the added capability or restores the previous model and application state. The pilot supports only the tested intervention.

title: 19  Choosing a viable deployment
text:
19.3 Model adaptation workflow
An adapted model or prompt can improve the target task while weakening a security property. The organization needs a controlled path from baseline to candidate version. A held-out test set is the general form of the evaluation holdout used in Chapters 3 and 4: it contains examples excluded from training and reserved for later evaluation. A security regression occurs when a security property becomes worse after a change. A known-good state is the recorded version that generalizes Chapter 4’s model baseline into a complete system state accepted for restoration.
NIST recommends renewed evaluation after a third-party model is fine-tuned and after adaptation to a new domain where earlier assumptions may fail.4 Secure-operation guidance also states that changes to data, models, or prompts can alter system behavior. It recommends versioning major updates and retaining a route to a known-good state.5 These recommendations do not specify one validation set or prove that re-evaluation prevents failure.
The process compares the candidate with the accepted baseline and records every security regression, including results on adversarial cases that the comparable evaluation in the next section will reuse. The release decision also references a rollback condition. A hypothetical support assistant might pass ordinary answer tests after fine-tuning but reveal restricted case details under adversarial prompts. The fine-tuned version would remain a candidate until that regression is understood. This workflow produces versioned alternatives for a comparable evaluation under shared permissions and quality targets.
Fine tuning can weaken model safeguards even when task quality improves. Qi and colleagues observed this effect after adversarial and ordinary fine-tuning in the models and data they tested.6 The deployment record links the base model, adaptation method, data version, training job, output weights or adapter, and both task and safety regression results. Isolation protects one organization’s adaptation data and credentials from another job. A comparison of parameter or adapter changes can help locate an unexpected change, but behavior tests remain necessary because a small numeric difference does not state its effect.
Control review. The release pipeline checks the candidate version against the held-out task set and the fixed security regression set, which includes adversarial cases matched to the deployment’s allowed data and action limits. It accepts the version only when every mandatory threshold passes. The report gives failures over all cases for each set and records review time and training cost. Data leakage into the held-out set or an untested attack can create a false pass, so the recorded sets apply only within their data and attacker assumptions. Recovery restores the known-good model, prompt, index, and runtime versions.

title: 19  Choosing a viable deployment
text:
19.4 Comparable deployment evaluation
A valid comparison gives each deployment the same task difficulty, permissions, and context allowance and measures it against the same quality target. A comparable evaluation tests alternatives with the same task set and decision criteria. A failure cost is the operational consequence assigned to an incorrect, unavailable, or unauthorized result. An adversarial case is a test in which an actor intentionally tries to cause a security failure.
The AI Risk Management Framework calls for validity and reliability under expected deployment conditions and for security and resilience to be evaluated and documented.7 It does not provide a complete head-to-head protocol. A worked comparison under constant workload, permissions, context size, quality target, and scoring rules remains an open need. Chapter 14 supplies the general evaluation method reused here.
For a hypothetical incident-triage task, all three candidates would receive the same redacted alerts, the same action prohibition, the same context allowance, and the same time window. Reviewers would measure accepted classifications against the shared quality target, unsafe disclosures, unauthorized action attempts, latency, and unavailable results, including results on the same adversarial cases. The resulting rates remain specific to that test set, permissions, and operating setup. They supply the quality and failure evidence needed for the cost model.
Measurement rule. The evaluation harness checks that every deployment receives the same case identifiers, context allowance, permissions, time window, acceptance rules, and adversarial cases. It rejects a comparison when any of those inputs differ. Each quality and failure rate uses all assigned cases as its denominator, while latency and reviewer effort use accepted results. A shared quality target is itself a test input: without it, a deployment could appear better by accepting lower quality. Comparable inputs may still omit a feature that matters in production or fail to represent future work. A failed comparison returns the pilot to the accepted baseline.

title: 19  Choosing a viable deployment
text:
19.5 Total ongoing cost
Purchase price alone can reverse a deployment decision once the system is operated. Unit cost divides the total cost recorded for a period by a defined unit of useful work. Fully loaded cost adds assigned infrastructure, labor, and operating cost to direct service cost. Capacity use is the share of available compute capacity doing useful work.
FinOps describes unit economics as a relationship between technology cost and business outcomes. Example units include cost per token, request, customer, transaction, or case resolved. Its more mature view includes fully loaded costs.8 The same guidance notes costs from data centers and enterprise agreements. Software services, model suppliers, and several cloud providers can add further costs.9 These categories organize the calculation. Actual prices and economic value require deployment evidence.
The calculation adds service charges or hardware depreciation, storage, network, energy, unused capacity, engineering labor, patching, monitoring, human review, and incident handling, including the staff and supplier cost of maintaining a managed platform. The denominator counts only results that meet the shared quality target and acceptance criteria. Actual prices, staffing effort, capacity use, and incident cost remain organization-specific inputs that require current evidence. This full cost view exposes the availability, fallback, and exit assumptions examined next.
Cost control. Finance and service records supply the period cost, while the evaluation record supplies accepted work for the same period and the same quality target. The decision rejects a unit-cost comparison when either period, acceptance rule, or quality target differs. Collection and allocation add accounting effort. Shared infrastructure, deferred maintenance, and rare incident costs can remain hidden. The recovery route is to recalculate with a stated range and reopen the deployment decision when actual cost crosses its condition. A lower unit cost does not establish lower risk or better continuity.
Comparable cost calculation. The following exercise values describe one year of the same read-only triage workload under the external and internal options. The managed option would split hardware and supplier charges between those extremes while retaining an external dependency for the host layer. Both illustrated options process 600,000 alerts and must meet the same quality threshold. Accepted work is the number of alert results that pass review. The values are hypothetical and use currency units rather than current supplier prices.



Table 19.1: Annual cost comparison.

The hosted unit cost is 414,000 divided by 570,000, or about 0.73 currency units per accepted result. The self-hosted unit cost is 547,000 divided by 576,000, or about 0.95. The self-hosted option accepts 6,000 more results in this example, but costs 133,000 more. Cost alone favors the hosted option. A managed deployment in this illustration would carry supplier host charges but keep model control internal, so its cost would fall between the two illustrated totals before staffing and exit cost are counted. Data-transfer limits, supplier exit, inspection needs, or a failed continuity test can still change the decision. The calculation is a comparison method, not evidence that any option has these costs in practice.
