title: 19  Choosing a viable deployment
text:
19.6 Operational constraints
An option with good test results and acceptable cost can still fail an operating requirement. An outbound dependency is an external service required during operation. A fallback is an alternate service or manual path used when the primary path fails. Exit cost is the work and cost required to leave a supplier or deployment design.
NIST recommends documenting dependence on third-party AI data and systems. It also recommends identifying fallbacks and testing rollover or manual procedures.10 Secure-development guidance also recommends recording where models, data, prompts, software, logs, and assessments are stored and retaining versions that permit restoration.11 The selected organization still needs legal analysis for location rules and system tests for continuity. A managed platform changes but does not remove these dependencies, because the host layer remains supplier-operated.
The final deployment record joins task quality under the shared quality target, rights, action limits, full cost per accepted result, required service level, fallback test results, and exit cost. A hypothetical internal model may remove an online supplier dependency while adding scarce operations staff and hardware recovery duties. A managed option reduces local hardware work but retains a supplier host dependency and its exit cost. A hosted service may reduce local maintenance while adding transfer and supplier-exit constraints. This bounded record becomes the input to organization-wide adoption in Chapter 20.
Continuity control. The service manager tests supplier loss and internal runtime loss against the same workload. The application routes work to the manual or deterministic fallback when the health check fails. The test reports completed fallback cases over all cases arriving during the disruption, time to switch, backlog, and total staff hours. Standby capacity and rehearsals raise ongoing cost. A shared identity, network, or data dependency can disable both paths. Because one exercise does not prove continuity for every outage duration, recovery restores the approved service and reconciles duplicate work. Normal routing resumes after credential verification.

Note
Chapter checkpoint. Choose between the two hypothetical deployments in the cost table. The pilot permits redacted alerts and prohibits response actions. It also requires a tested manual fallback under the same quality target and permissions. State the decision and one condition that would reopen it.
Conclusion. The hosted option is the current choice because it meets the stated task and quality target while producing the lower cost per accepted result. The approval remains limited to redacted, read-only triage under the tested permissions and adversarial conditions. A failed supplier-exit test, a change in transfer rules, or evidence that local inspection is required would reopen the decision. This conclusion does not claim that a hosted service is generally safer or cheaper.


Starter literature. These sources provide the initial evidence base for the chapter and guide later research, but they do not support every claim by themselves. 12 13

title: Part VII: Governing organizational AI
text:
Chapters in this part
Organizational AI governance depends on visible uses, responsible parties, decisions, and unresolved risks.
The organization inventory connects approved and unapproved uses to accounts, connectors, data, suppliers, and review dates. Responsibility records assign authority and duties. Exposure, outcome, and cost measures then support security investment decisions.

title: Part VII: Governing organizational AI
text:
Managing organizational AI use: An organization-wide adoption process connects visible AI uses to acceptable-use rules, account and connector controls, and employee support.
Assigning responsibility: A responsibility map assigns decisions and evidence across developers, providers, deployers, data owners, purchasers, and affected people.
Choosing security investments: An investment decision connects measures, evidence, responsible owners, review dates, and remaining risk to staff, money, and time.

title: 20  Managing organizational AI use
text:
20.1 Organizational AI inventory
Security question. How can an organization allow useful AI work without losing sight of systems, data, permissions, and changes?
Organization setting. Suppose employees use approved assistants, purchased software with AI features, and some unapproved services.
One approved assistant is only one entry in an organization’s AI inventory. Each additional service or embedded feature needs its own task, data, connector, action, supplier, and review record.
Policy cannot govern an AI use that the organization cannot see. An enterprise AI inventory is a controlled record of AI systems and AI-enabled services used by the organization. An embedded AI feature is an AI capability included inside another purchased product. A data flow records movement of data among users, systems, suppliers, and stores.
The NIST Cybersecurity Framework (CSF) 2.0 separates inventories of software, services, supplier services, data, metadata, and authorized internal and external data flows.1 The AI Risk Management Framework also includes maintaining an inventory of AI systems according to organizational risk priorities.2 Completeness and currentness require separate discovery evidence.
For each entry, the record links the business task, responsible owner, users, model or service, data types, connectors, data flows, action permissions, supplier, and review date. Discovery may combine procurement and identity records. Expense data, network observations, and employee reports add other views. These are common inventory practices, and their coverage depends on the available evidence. The resulting population defines which uses the acceptable-use rules govern.
Inventory trace. The hypothetical organization compares four discovery inputs for one month: procurement lists an approved assistant and identity logs show two AI services. Expense records show a third service, while an employee report identifies an AI feature inside a support product. The intermediate state is a reconciliation table with service identity, business task, data class, connector, responsible role, and review date. One expense entry has no responsible role and one embedded feature has no data-flow record. The observed result is four candidate uses, two complete records, and two unresolved records. The conclusion treats the inventory as evidence-linked records with visible gaps. It does not claim completeness.
Inventory control. The service that maintains the inventory reconciles procurement, identity, expense, network, and employee reports and marks incomplete entries for review. It allows onboarding only for a record with the required task, data, connector, responsible role, and review date. Coverage is confirmed records divided by all candidate uses found through the stated inputs. Discovery and reconciliation require staff time and can miss personal accounts or hidden product features. Because high coverage across these inputs does not prove that every AI use has been found, recovery suspends unresolved connectors or routes the task to an approved service.

title: 20  Managing organizational AI use
text:
20.2 Acceptable use rules
A general instruction to “use AI responsibly” does not tell an employee if a real task is allowed. An acceptable-use rule sets conditions on permitted AI tasks, data, outputs, or actions. A consequential output can materially affect a person, asset, obligation, or decision. A safe alternative is an approved method offered when the requested AI use is restricted.
NIST recommends updating generative AI acceptable-use policies to cover proprietary and open-source technology and data, as well as contractors and other third parties.3 This is governance guidance, not a complete policy or evidence that publication alone changes behavior.
Rule trace. In a hypothetical case, employee A12 submits four separate requests. The first request covers a public policy summary in the approved assistant. The second covers pasting customer record C44 into an unapproved service. The third covers generating a contract clause. The fourth covers executing a refund payment. The check evaluates task, data class, target service, and requested action against the inventory record for the approved assistant. The observed results are public summary allowed and customer paste blocked by a field filter with a safe alternative to the restricted internal assistant. The contract clause is allowed only with a legal-review flag, and the payment execution is blocked. The trace shows that the rule becomes enforceable only when account and connector permissions match it.
Use control. The application and connector check the employee identity, task, data class, target service, and requested action. They either allow the request or block it. A field filter can change the request before the application shows the safe alternative. Tests report blocked prohibited cases and blocked allowed cases over all policy cases. Classification, support, and exception handling add cost and delay. Copying data through an unmanaged device or misclassifying a field can bypass the rule. Recovery revokes exposed access and removes retained data where the service permits. Work then moves to the approved path. A passed policy test does not prove employee behavior outside managed channels.

title: 20  Managing organizational AI use
text:
20.3 Accounts and connectors
An approved service can still exceed policy if a broad connector or shared account bypasses individual access limits. A connector is an integration that lets an AI application read from or act on another system. The security decision identifies the human or service identity used for each call. Its permission scope states the resources and operations allowed to that identity.
CSF 2.0 calls for identities and credentials for users, services, and hardware to be managed. It also calls for permissions and authorizations to be defined, enforced, reviewed, and limited through least privilege and separation of duties.4 These outcomes do not specify an identity product or prove that a connector applies the intended rule.
This identity chain applies from employee onboarding through offboarding. The application authenticates the employee, the connector uses a distinct service identity or delegated token, the target service performs a current authorization check, and logs connect the request to both identities. Shared credentials break this chain. Review dates and revocation tests show whether access changes take effect. These details provide concrete evidence for procurement and onboarding.
Revocation test. In this hypothetical test, employee E17 loses access to customer case C44 at 10:00. At 10:05 the employee submits a request for a C44 summary. The application stores an earlier conversation, but the connector sends E17’s current identity to the case system. The case system denies access, so the application records the denial without receiving the customer record. The observed result meets the expected result. If the connector had used a shared service account and returned the record, the test would show that approval of the AI service did not enforce the employee’s current permissions.
Control review. The target case system enforces access from the current employee identity and record identifier. The connector passes through the denial and clears any queued result for that record. A revocation test reports denied former permissions over all revoked user-resource pairs, plus time from source revocation to effective denial. Delegated identity and frequent checks add integration and latency cost. Cached content, shared credentials, or a second connector can bypass the path. Because one successful pair does not establish complete offboarding, recovery purges affected caches and revokes connector tokens before the full revoked set is retested.

title: 20  Managing organizational AI use
text:
20.4 Procurement and onboarding
A supplier review has little value when it examines a brand while leaving the intended use, data, and actions unspecified. A pilot limit is a temporary restriction on users, data, actions, duration, or scale during evaluation. Supplier due diligence examines the supplier before a relationship begins. A time-limited exception is an approved deviation that expires or requires renewed review.
NIST recommends procurement checks for intellectual property, privacy, security, embedded AI, ongoing monitoring, model and tool changes, and incident or vulnerability records.5 CSF 2.0 also calls for due diligence before a supplier relationship and continued recording, treatment, and monitoring of supplier risk.6 These lists do not certify a supplier or settle sector-specific contract duties.
The onboarding record ties the use case to permitted data, action limits, identity design, supplier evidence, acceptance tests, pilot expiry, and an accountable decision. A time-limited exception records why an ordinary requirement cannot yet be met and when renewed review occurs. The people operating the approved use then need task-specific competence and a practical route for help.
Onboarding trace. The hypothetical review examines a help-desk assistant that will summarize policy and draft replies using a supplier service with a read-only policy-store connector. The inputs are the use record with task, data types, connector and permission scope, supplier evidence, and required contract terms. The reviewer checks pilot limits for 80 users and 90 days, acceptance tests for blocked customer fields and revocation, and expiry for the pending data-processing addendum. The observed result is a restricted approval with the customer-field block, monthly review, and a time-limited exception that expires at the addendum date. The decision, responsible owner, and review date enter the inventory before the connector is enabled.
Approval control. A procurement reviewer checks the use record, supplier scope, required contract terms, pilot limits, test results, exception expiry, and decision authority. The reviewer approves, restricts, or postpones onboarding. The review reports complete approvals over all proposed uses and overdue exceptions over all active exceptions. Supplier review and negotiation consume legal and engineering time. A product update or unreported subprocessor can invalidate the evidence after approval. Recovery disables the feature or connector and returns users to the stated alternative while review is renewed. Approval does not certify the supplier beyond the inspected service and period.

title: 20  Managing organizational AI use
text:
20.5 Employee skills and support
Employees encounter the system at the point where an unreliable answer, suspicious instruction, or unexpected request becomes a business decision. Human oversight assigns review or intervention to a person with sufficient authority and support. A help channel is a specified route for advice, reporting, or escalation. Training needs to match the assigned task and the decisions the employee can make.
CSF 2.0 distinguishes general awareness from training for specialized roles, with both tied to the knowledge and skills needed to perform work while considering cybersecurity risk.7 Subject to its scope and phased application dates, the European Union AI Act sets a duty for deployers of covered high-risk systems to assign human oversight to people with suitable competence, training, authority, and support.8 That legal rule is limited to the systems and dates covered by the Act.
A hypothetical customer-support employee may need to verify a refund instruction through the case system, while an administrator needs to inspect connector permissions and logs. Questions and incident reports pass through the help channel, so employees do not have to guess. Reports, repeated confusion, and support demand become evidence for adoption and change review.
Competence check. The employee receives a synthetic message that asks for a refund and includes an assistant-generated bank-account change. The task is to decide what can proceed. The expected path ignores the generated payment instruction and verifies the case in the authoritative support system. The account change then goes to the established review channel. The observed exercise result records the employee’s choice, the evidence consulted, and whether escalation occurred. A correct answer supports competence for this scenario only. It does not show readiness for administration, incident response, or legal review.
Oversight control. The business workflow requires the authoritative record and the specified approval role before a consequential change can proceed. The competence test reports correct decisions over all assigned scenarios and records unsafe approvals and unnecessary escalations separately. Training, review, and support time are operating costs. Time pressure, ambiguous cases, or an unavailable help channel can defeat the human step. Recovery stops the transaction and uses the ordinary manual process. Staff review any action already taken. A high exercise score does not prove reliable performance during real incidents.

title: 20  Managing organizational AI use
text:
20.6 Adoption and change review
High use does not by itself show that adoption is safe or valuable. An adoption measure is a count or rate describing approved use of an AI capability. Policy friction is delay or work created by a policy during ordinary tasks. A retirement trigger is an observed condition that starts removal or replacement review.
CSF 2.0 calls for policy review when requirements, threats, technology, or mission change. It also calls for changes and exceptions to be assessed, recorded, and tracked.9 The framework does not define AI adoption measures or universal retirement thresholds. The evidence packet also lacks validated examples of measures that avoid rewarding unsafe volume or discouraging incident reporting.
The review keeps that limit visible. A rise in reports can reflect growing abuse or better awareness. Both causes may be present. Low use can reflect poor value or excessive friction, while incomplete discovery offers another explanation. New model capabilities, contract terms, connectors, or data access can invalidate the original approval even when usage is stable. The resulting practice, exceptions, and open questions become inputs to the responsibility analysis in Chapter 21.
Adoption review record. The example below uses hypothetical values for one quarterly review.

The reviewer compares observed use with the approved task, data, accounts, connectors, and support route. The conclusion is to continue the policy summary pilot with a block on customer fields and focused employee support. The proposed email connector remains outside approval because it changes available data and actions.
Change control. The application configuration checks the approved connector list and data rules before enabling a supplier feature. The review board checks new capabilities, terms, regions, permissions, and incident results before expanding the approval. Measures use changed systems over all inventoried approved systems and policy violations over all inspected requests. Review and field filtering create cost and user friction. Supplier-side activation or incomplete inventory data can bypass the gate. Because stable usage and answer quality do not prove that the boundary remained unchanged, recovery disables the added capability and restores the accepted configuration. Work moves to the documented fallback.

Note
Chapter checkpoint. A supplier update adds an email connector to an approved assistant that summarizes policy. Usage and answer quality remain unchanged. Can the existing approval continue without review?
Answer. No. The connector changes the data flow, possible content, and account permissions even though usage and answer quality did not change. The adoption record should mark the connector as outside the approved boundary and keep it disabled. The record must also identify the responsible role and tests required for a new decision.

title: 21  Assigning responsibility
text:
21.1 Roles and responsibilities
Security question. Who is responsible for each AI system decision, and which legal, contractual, and governance duties apply?
Organization setting. Suppose an organization buys model access and builds an application around it. The application connects internal data and serves employees or customers. Several parties can affect the same outcome, but their authority and duties differ.
The inventory shows which parties operate components and make decisions. Responsibility follows those acts and authorities, while legal and contractual duties depend on use, location, role, and date.
Responsibility becomes unclear when a project calls every outside party a vendor and every internal party an owner. The analysis begins with the act each party performs. Under the EU AI Act, a provider develops or has an AI system or general-purpose AI model developed and places it on the market, or puts an AI system into service, under its own name or trademark. A deployer uses an AI system under its authority, excluding personal, non-professional use.1 An affected person is a person whose rights, safety, access, or interests may be affected.
Those are legal roles under the European Union AI Act, not general labels for every supplier and user. For covered high-risk systems, branding, substantial modification, or a change in intended purpose can cause another party to assume provider obligations.2 These definitions apply only within the Act’s scope and dates. A project still needs a system-specific responsibility map that separates internal and external parties.
The map links each lifecycle decision to authority, evidence, and escalation. An external supplier may operate inference. The internal application team selects the data and grants connector access. An internal business owner decides if an output affects a customer. An affected person may have no operating role but still requires consideration in risk decisions. The role map identifies which obligations need examination next.
Responsibility trace. In the hypothetical employee assistant, the external supplier operates model inference, the internal application team selects retrieved fields, and the internal identity service checks the employee’s access. The internal support director has authority over whether a proposed account change can enter the business process, while the internal Chief Security Officer accepts the specified residual security risk. The intermediate record links each act to one responsible role and one evidence source. A supplier report cannot approve the organization’s connector permissions. A technical test cannot replace the authorized business-risk decision. The conclusion is that responsibility follows the act and authority, not a general label applied to the whole system.
Responsibility control. The decision workflow checks that each consequential act has one responsible role, stated authority, evidence source, escalation route, and review date. It holds approval when any field is missing or conflicting. The measure is complete assignments divided by all consequential acts in the system map. Maintaining the map and resolving conflicts take staff time. Informal decisions outside the workflow can bypass it. Recovery withdraws the unsupported decision and escalates it to a role with authority. A complete assignment shows who must decide, not that the decision is correct.

title: 21  Assigning responsibility
text:
21.2 Applicable obligations
The same technical system can face different duties when its use, location, operator, or date changes. A jurisdiction is a legal territory whose rules may apply. Legal scope is the set of facts that brings a person, organization, system, or act under a rule. An effective date is the date from which a provision applies.
The consolidated EU AI Act text applies generally from August 2, 2026, while amended Article 113 sets later dates for specified Annex III and Annex I systems.3 Dates differ across provisions, so one headline date cannot replace provision-level checking. In the United States health setting, the Department of Health and Human Services stated in its August 7, 2026 review that the current Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act Security Rule remained in effect. Proposed cybersecurity changes had not become a final rule.4
These examples show the process rather than a global legal survey. A final decision needs current primary law and qualified interpretation for the organization’s actual locations and sector. Once binding duties and contract terms are identified, voluntary frameworks can organize the remaining work without being mistaken for law.
Scope trace. The organization records five inputs before applying a rule: operating location, user location, affected person, intended use, and decision date. A hypothetical credit-scoring use and an internal alert-triage use share a model supplier but have different intended purposes. The internal legal reviewer checks the current provision and effective date for each use. The intermediate record marks the credit use for provision-level analysis and leaves the alert-triage use outside that specific classification pending other duties. The observed result is a scoped question. It does not classify the model in general.
Dated scope gate. The legal reviewer checks the five inputs against current primary text and records the provision, date, reviewer, and unresolved facts. The reviewer either allows or postpones the proposed use, and an allowed use can carry limits. Coverage is reviewed obligations divided by all candidate obligations identified for the use. Qualified review, updates, and supplier fact gathering create ongoing cost. A stale summary, changed use, or missing location can invalidate the result. Because the record does not prove compliance beyond its facts, law, and date, recovery pauses the affected function and preserves the prior permitted path. The internal owner then repeats the legal review with current facts.

title: 21  Assigning responsibility
text:
21.3 Frameworks and standards
A framework organizes outcomes or practices used to structure risk work without specifying one way to carry them out. CSF 2.0 presents a technology-neutral hierarchy of cybersecurity outcomes and states that it does not prescribe how organizations achieve them.5 It can connect risk work across teams, but it is not an AI control catalogue and does not demonstrate control quality.
A management system is a connected set of policies, roles, processes, and reviews used to meet organizational objectives. The public ISO page describes ISO/IEC 42001 as requirements for establishing, implementing, maintaining, and continually improving an AI management system.6 Clause-level claims require the licensed normative text, so the public page supports only this scope description.
An organization may use a crosswalk, a scoped mapping between related items in different sources. It records the relationship and the gap instead of treating differently scoped documents as interchangeable. Those categories now guide the data, documentation, supplier, and contract questions in the remaining sections.
Crosswalk comparison. The organization starts with the concrete decision “Who can expand the assistant to customer data?” CSF 2.0 supplies outcomes for responsibility, supplier risk, and access control. The AI Risk Management Framework supplies AI context, measurement, and risk-management questions. ISO/IEC 42001 supplies management-system requirements only to the extent available in the licensed text. The intermediate crosswalk records the relevant item, the system evidence, and any uncovered question. The observed gap is the actual legal basis for customer-data use. No framework row fills that gap. The conclusion is that a crosswalk organizes evidence but does not turn guidance into law or prove compliance.
Crosswalk control. The review register checks every selected framework or standard item against a concrete system record and marks missing evidence or scope. It prevents a framework row from closing a legal or technical question that the source does not answer. Coverage is supported mappings divided by all mappings used in the decision. Building and maintaining the register costs review time. Broad labels and copied mappings can hide a gap. Recovery reopens the affected decision and obtains the missing source or test. A complete crosswalk shows organized coverage, not control effectiveness or legal compliance.

title: 21  Assigning responsibility
text:
21.4 Data and intellectual property rights
Data can be technically accessible while still being unavailable for collection, training, retrieval, or reuse. Collection permission is the legal, contractual, or organizational basis for obtaining data. A reuse right permits use of material for a later purpose. Confidential information is information protected from unauthorized disclosure by duty or agreement.
NIST recommends categorizing generative AI content by third-party rights and setting policies for how third-party intellectual property and training data are used, stored, and protected.7 This guidance identifies governance work. It does not decide ownership, infringement, fair use, database rights, trade secrets, privacy duties, or license enforcement.
A hypothetical organization may have permission to store a customer document for service delivery but no permission to use it for model training. Retrieval for an authorized employee may also differ from disclosure to an external model supplier. Current jurisdiction-specific primary law and qualified interpretation remain necessary for substantive legal conclusions. The permissions and restrictions determine which decision and change records need to remain available.
Permission control. The internal data gateway checks the data class, person or service identity, intended purpose, destination, retention rule, and recorded permission before collection, retrieval, training, or external transfer. It allows, removes fields, or blocks the operation and logs the basis. Tests report allowed and denied flows over all purpose-destination cases. Classification and legal review add cost. Copied data, wrong labels, or supplier reuse outside the observed interface can defeat the control. Recovery revokes access and removes affected copies where possible. Rights questions receive qualified review. A technical denial does not settle the underlying legal interpretation.

title: 21  Assigning responsibility
text:
21.5 Documentation and oversight
A responsible role cannot review a system if the reason for a decision disappeared with a meeting. A decision record captures the options, evidence, responsible role, date, conditions, and unresolved issues behind a decision. Related records describe the system, tests, oversight authority, access, incidents, and changes.
The AI Risk Management Framework connects system context, intended purpose, task, legal risk, human oversight, testing, and lifecycle decisions across its MAP, MEASURE, and MANAGE functions.8 For covered high-risk systems, the EU AI Act connects technical documentation, automated logging, information for deployers, human oversight, and deployer monitoring duties.9 These sources do not establish one record format or universal retention period.
The documentation set follows the system boundary. It links versions and decisions without claiming that the record itself proves the system is safe. A human oversight assignment identifies the person or role with review and intervention authority. A change record preserves evidence of a system change and its assessment. These records supply the questions and evidence requests used in supplier assurance.
Decision-record test. A model version changes on 4 October in this hypothetical case. The prior internal record approved version V7 for policy summaries with read-only retrieval. The change record identifies version V8, the external supplier notice, affected tests, responsible internal reviewer, and the decision to hold expansion. The team can trace each test result back to V7 or V8. If the record contained only “model updated,” a later reviewer could not tell which evidence remained relevant. The observed result tests whether the documentation supports a decision rather than whether a form was completed.
Change control. The internal release workflow checks the system version, affected assumptions, required tests, oversight assignment, and approval before routing users to the change. It either allows release or keeps the accepted version. A release can carry restrictions. The measure is fully linked material changes divided by all detected material changes. Version tracking and review delay delivery. An emergency change or silent external supplier update can bypass the workflow, and complete documentation still cannot show that every failure was detected. Recovery restores the accepted configuration and reconstructs missing records from internal logs and supplier notices.

title: 21  Assigning responsibility
text:
21.6 Supplier assurance
A certificate or audit title can appear relevant while covering the wrong service, location, control period, or customer configuration. Assurance scope identifies the systems, services, locations, controls, and period covered by evidence. A subprocessor is another party used by a supplier to process data or deliver service. The review also records exclusions, shared responsibilities, and customer actions required for the assurance to apply.
CSF 2.0 calls for coordination of supplier roles and inclusion of security requirements in contracts. It also calls for due diligence before a relationship and risk monitoring during it.10 NIST also recommends contract clauses that permit evaluation of third-party generative AI processes and standards.11 A service-specific review still needs to establish the audit quality and the relevance of supplier controls to the organization’s system.
The evidence packet lacks a strong public source on detailed scope and customer-control sections in common assurance reports. The gap remains. The internal review compares the assurance scope with the actual data flow and service configuration, then lists every uncovered dependency. Those gaps become contract and exit requirements.
Supplier-scope comparison. The hypothetical external supplier report covers inference service S1 in region R1 for January through June. The organization uses S1 in region R2 from August and supplies its own internal connector. The internal reviewer records the service, region, period, supplier control, and customer control in the comparison. The observed gaps are region R2, the later operating period, and the customer connector. The report may still provide useful evidence for covered controls, but it cannot support a conclusion about the uncovered configuration. The responsible internal role requests current evidence and records the connector as an organization duty.
Assurance control. The internal procurement gate compares service, region, period, configuration, subprocessors, supplier controls, and customer duties with the actual deployment. It either accepts the evidence or leaves the related use unapproved. Acceptance can carry a condition. Coverage is matched scope items divided by all scope items required for the decision. Obtaining and reviewing evidence adds supplier and internal cost. A stale report or omitted customer control can produce a false assurance. Recovery restricts the service and disables the uncovered path. Work can move to the approved fallback. A matched report supports only its stated scope and does not prove the whole application secure.

title: 21  Assigning responsibility
text:
21.7 Contract and exit provisions
Dependence becomes difficult to change after data, connectors, workflows, and staff practices accumulate around one service. Portability is the ability to move data, configurations, and necessary artifacts to another service. Termination assistance is supplier support for an orderly end or transfer. A continuity term is a contract condition intended to preserve essential operations during disruption or exit.
NIST recommends reviewing AI supplier contracts for termination, responsibility, incident notice, response times, support availability, and service levels.12 CSF 2.0 includes supplier participation in incident activity and risk management after a service agreement ends.13 These are governance outcomes. Contract language and enforceability require separate legal work.
A hypothetical exit test exports allowed records and removes connector access. It then revokes service credentials and checks deletion evidence. The fallback workflow runs after those checks. Jurisdiction-specific clauses and evidence about practical exit testing remain open research needs. The resulting responsibility, supplier, and continuity record provides the input for security investment decisions in Chapter 22.
Exit control. The exit workflow checks required data, configurations, logs, open cases, credentials, supplier deletion evidence, and fallback readiness. It completes termination only after each item is transferred, retained under an approved basis, or recorded as unresolved. Measures include recovered required items over all required items and revoked credentials over all active credentials. Portability tests, standby service, and supplier support add ongoing cost. Proprietary formats, supplier delay, or a shared dependency can block exit. Recovery keeps the manual path active and limits new data while unresolved items are escalated. A supplier deletion statement does not by itself prove removal from every copy.

Note
Chapter checkpoint. A supplier operates inference, the organization selects customer data, and an internal support director approves account changes. Assign responsibility for model service operation, retrieval eligibility, and the final account decision. State one evidence item and one limit for each assignment.
Answer. The external supplier is responsible for the contracted operation of the model service, supported by service records and limited to the contract and assurance scope. The internal organization role that controls retrieval is responsible for eligible customer fields, supported by permission and retrieval tests and limited by current law and data rights. The internal support director is responsible for the account decision under the organization’s authority, supported by approval and action logs and limited by the director’s approval range. Each assignment remains limited to its stated act and authority.

title: 22  Choosing security investments
text:
22.1 Program ownership
Security question. How can leaders decide which AI security work receives staff, money, and time?
Organization setting. Suppose an organization operates several AI uses with different data, permissions, suppliers, consequences, and evidence quality. Leaders cannot fund every proposed control at once.
Assurance, monitoring, deployment, adoption, and responsibility records compete for limited staff, money, and time. Investment choices need measures of exposure, outcomes, uncertainty, and control cost.
A register full of risks and controls does not create a decision. Each asset, use case, exception, escalation, and review needs a person with authority to act. An accountable owner can accept or escalate a result. The same person can require more work before deciding. Risk acceptance records a decision to retain specified residual risk. Review frequency sets an interval or event rule for reassessment.
CSF 2.0 places accountability with organizational leadership. It calls for cybersecurity roles, responsibilities, and authorities to be established, understood, and enforced, with resources allocated in line with risk strategy.1 These outcomes do not select one organization chart.
The program record connects each owner to a decision and a review rule. A technical lead may own a test result, while the Chief Security Officer may own escalation and an executive may have authority to accept residual risk. The record states the boundary instead of treating “ownership” as a vague label. These assignments give each coverage measure a reader and a purpose.
Program control. The governance workflow checks each active system, exception, escalation, and risk decision for an authorized role and a current review rule. It blocks expansion or risk acceptance when either is missing. Coverage is complete assignments divided by all active decision records. Maintaining the register and resolving authority conflicts consume staff time for reviews, calendar time for escalation windows, and budget for governance tooling. Informal approval or an incomplete inventory can bypass the workflow. Recovery pauses the affected decision and escalates it to the correct authority. A complete register does not show that the selected control is effective.

title: 22  Choosing security investments
text:
22.2 Coverage and exposure measures
A count such as “twenty systems reviewed” has no clear meaning without the total population. A coverage measure combines a numerator with the full population that the count is meant to represent. Examples include reviewed high-impact systems divided by all known high-impact systems, or tested sensitive connectors divided by all sensitive connectors in the inventory.
NIST distinguishes measures showing progress in putting controls in place from effectiveness, efficiency, and impact measures.2 It also states that the source, collection method, and validation process for measurement data need definition so results can be repeated and compared over time.3 Repeatable data does not make an irrelevant measure useful, and high control coverage does not establish control effectiveness.
The mechanism starts with an inventory and a clear denominator. An overdue exception is an approved deviation whose review or expiry date has passed. The measure records missing items, exclusions, stale records, and overdue exceptions instead of silently dropping them. A hypothetical result of 90 tested connectors out of 100 known connectors shows 90 percent coverage. It says nothing yet about the ten untested connectors or the quality of the tests. Outcome measures, described in the next section, address that different question, and Chapter 20 provides the inventory method that supplies the denominator.
Coverage decision. The reporting service checks connector inventory status, test date, result, exception, and expiry. The responsible role can continue, restrict, or pause use based on a stated threshold. The denominator includes every known connector in scope, including failed, untested, and excepted items. Collection and follow-up add operating cost in staff hours for discovery, money for inventory tooling, and time until the next refresh. Unknown connectors and stale inventories can inflate the rate, while 90 percent coverage still says nothing about the amount of risk reduction. Recovery adds missing items and tests the unresolved population before the decision is reissued.

title: 22  Choosing security investments
text:
22.3 Security outcome measures
Completion counts describe work performed. An outcome measure observes the result a control is meant to change. A rate divides an event count by a relevant exposure or opportunity count. Recovery time is elapsed time from a specified disruption point to a specified restored state.
NIST describes effectiveness measures as evidence of how well controls meet desired outcomes, efficiency measures as the speed of useful feedback and correction, and impact measures as effects on mission, cost, value, penalties, or trust.4 It also states that one measure may be insufficient for a risk decision and that resource limits prevent measuring everything.5 These categories do not supply AI-specific measures or establish that a control caused an observed change.
Every result reports its denominator. A harmful-action count has a different meaning across one hundred authorized calls than across one million. Prevented attempts, duplicate events, incomplete reports, and changed exposure can also alter the rate. The packet lacks a validated worked denominator for these cases, so the examples require testing before operational use. The measured outcomes then inform renewed assessment and change decisions, as defined in Chapter 14 and observed in Chapter 15.
Outcome control. The measurement pipeline joins action, denial, incident, recovery, and exposure records for the same period and configuration. It reports harmful completed actions over all eligible action attempts, plus missing or duplicate records. A threshold can trigger restriction or renewed testing. Instrumentation and investigation add cost in logging infrastructure, analyst time, and time to triage. Logging gaps can hide failures. Recovery repairs the data path and recomputes the measure. Earlier decisions remain uncertain until review. A changed rate does not by itself prove that one control caused the change.

title: 22  Choosing security investments
text:
22.4 Assurance and change decisions
An approval is tied to the system and evidence that existed at the time. A material change is large enough to invalidate an assumption, test, approval, or duty. A renewed assessment repeats review after a trigger. A release condition is an evidence threshold required before deployment or expansion.
CSF 2.0 calls for improvements to be identified from evaluations, security tests and exercises, operational work, and incident planning.6 NIST’s generative AI profile recommends renewed model risk review after fine-tuning or adaptation to a new domain.7 These sources identify triggers but do not set a universal release threshold or prove that a proposed improvement works.
The decision record links each trigger to stale evidence and the required renewed assessment. It also identifies the authority that can pause or expand use. A minor interface change may need a focused regression test. A new action permission may reopen the threat model and authorization tests. It may also require a new incident plan and legal review, as assigned in Chapter 21. These decisions create evidence-based options for investment prioritization.
Change gate. The release service checks the component version, permission change, supplier notice, affected assumptions, required tests, and decision authority. It either permits the change or keeps the prior version. Permission can carry limits. The measure is reviewed material changes divided by all detected material changes, with failed tests retained in the count. Review and rollback capacity increase ongoing cost in staff time for assessment, money for duplicate environments, and calendar time for retesting. Silent supplier changes and untracked configuration can bypass the gate. Recovery restores the accepted version and repeats affected tests. Passing those tests supports only the changed paths and cases they cover.

title: 22  Choosing security investments
text:
22.5 Security investment choices
Exposure alone gives an incomplete priority. A priority decision uses business value, possible harm, and uncertainty. Control cost, legal duty, and displaced work also affect it. Expected loss is a probability-weighted estimate of adverse impact, but rare AI events may leave both probability and impact highly uncertain. Opportunity cost is the value of work displaced by the selected investment.
NIST says measurement priorities can consider risk strategy, mission, data availability, asset value, control cost, partial controls, risk assessments, policy, and legal requirements.8 It also says likelihood and impact need to be considered together because either alone is insufficient for deciding the importance of a potential measure.9 The guidance does not provide a universal scoring formula or validate probability estimates for rare events.
The decision can use ranges and scenarios when point estimates would imply false precision. A control required by law may remain mandatory even when its expected-loss estimate is small. A cheap control with broad benefit may receive priority over a costly control aimed at a narrow, uncertain scenario. The selected priorities and their uncertainty need a durable executive record.
Investment comparison. The hypothetical organization has 180,000 currency units and two optional projects after funding its required controls. Project A limits connector permissions for six assistants. It costs 110,000 in budget, needs two engineers for three weeks and three review days, and addresses a tested path that reached restricted records in 4 of 200 adversarial cases (2 percent, with a wide uncertainty range because the sample is small). Project B adds a model-behavior filter to one public assistant. It costs 150,000, needs one engineer for four weeks plus ongoing tuning time, and addresses a plausible misuse scenario for which no local rate is yet available. These exercise values support only the comparison and do not measure control effectiveness.
The intermediate decision record compares affected systems, observed evidence, possible harm, delivery cost in money, staff, and time, displaced work, and uncertainty. Project A has direct local evidence and broader system coverage. Project B may address serious harm, but the organization first needs a focused test that measures the path and the filter under its actual application conditions, as evaluated in Chapter 14. The current conclusion funds Project A and reserves 70,000 plus two engineer-weeks for that test and other unresolved work. A legal duty from Chapter 21 or stronger evidence could change the order.
Investment control. The portfolio review board checks each option for affected systems, required duty, evidence quality, cost range in money, staff, and time, displaced work, bypass risk, and recovery benefit. The board funds, postpones, or rejects the option and records the condition that reopens it. Coverage is funded required controls over all required controls, while optional work retains its uncertainty range. Analysis and delayed projects have real cost in analyst hours, budget committed, and opportunity time lost. Optimistic estimates or missing systems can distort the order, and the ranking does not establish that the funded control will achieve its expected effect. Recovery reserves capacity for newly observed failures and repeats the comparison when a condition changes.

title: 22  Choosing security investments
text:
22.6 Executive decision records
A funding, expansion, pause, or acceptance decision needs enough context to be reviewed after staff, suppliers, or evidence change. Residual risk is the risk remaining after the selected measures. A decision condition is an event or threshold that changes an approval. A due date sets the date by which an action or review is expected.
NIST measurement guidance says a report can state the indicated risk and its fit with risk appetite. The report can also identify the needed decision and compliance concerns. It can record audit effects separately.10 CSF 2.0 calls for oversight results to adjust strategy and for risk responses to be selected, prioritized, tracked, and communicated.11 Legal and organizational authority determine who may accept a specific risk.
A decision condition makes approval contingent on an event or threshold. Expansion may depend on completing permission tests and resolving two critical supplier gaps. A due date keeps a temporary exception from becoming permanent through neglect. Teams can reuse the record and its reasoning in the sector cases in Chapter 23 and the whole-system review in Chapter 25.
Executive record trace. The decision record for Project A identifies the Chief Security Officer as the decision role, the six affected assistants, the 4 of 200 test result with its small-sample uncertainty, the 110,000 exercise cost, two engineers for three weeks, three review days, and the remaining risk from untested connectors. It approves the work for the six systems and requires a repeated authorization test before expansion. The application team is responsible for delivery by 30 November. A new action connector or a failed regression test pauses expansion and returns the decision for review. The observed output is a conditional funding decision that another reviewer can reconstruct from its inputs and limits.
Decision control. Before approval, the executive decision workflow checks the responsible authority, evidence date, scope, cost in money, staff, and time, due date, residual risk, and stop condition before recording approval. It rejects a record that lacks any required field. Quality is reconstructable decisions divided by all consequential decisions reviewed in the period. Preparation and challenge sessions consume leadership and technical time. Decisions made outside the record or based on stale evidence can bypass the check. Recovery suspends the affected approval and returns it to the stated role. Reconstructability does not prove that the judgment was optimal.

Note
Chapter checkpoint. The organization can fund Project B only by cancelling the test reserved in the Project A decision. Should it do so when Project B has higher possible harm but no local exposure or control-effectiveness result?
Conclusion. The present record does not support cancelling the test. Possible harm matters, but the missing exposure and effectiveness evidence prevents a comparable investment decision. The organization should keep required controls funded and complete the focused test. It should also record the condition that would move Project B ahead. This answer applies to the hypothetical evidence and budget, not to every high-impact risk.

title: Part VIII: Adapting controls to change
text:
Chapters in this part
Controls and evidence can lose validity when the sector, operating conditions, or system capabilities change.
Sector cases change data, authority, duties, scale, and possible harm. Technical cases change physical access, participant trust, persistence, delegation, or capability. A shared final case combines the affected controls and evidence in one reviewable decision.
crumbs: Part VIII: Adapting controls to change

title: Part VIII: Adapting controls to change
text:
Adapting controls by sector: A transfer review states which assets, duties, permissions, and consequences change before applying earlier controls to a new sector.
Security under changed assumptions: Changes in physical access, participant trust, persistence, delegated authority, or systemic uncertainty reopen earlier security assumptions.
Reviewing a system decision: A whole system review connects architecture, data, model and platform controls, authority, assurance, recovery, cost, and accountability in one decision.
crumbs: Part VIII: Adapting controls to change

title: 23  Adapting controls by sector
text:
23.1 Enterprise support assistants
Security question. Which assumptions, controls, and evidence change when the users, data, authority, and consequences change?
Organization setting. Each case is hypothetical. The examples isolate design differences and do not establish legal compliance, clinical safety, financial fitness, or product security.
The same technical control can have different value in enterprise support, health, finance, public services, and consumer platforms. Assets, permissions, duties, scale, consequences, oversight depth, and recovery evidence determine what changes.
The enterprise, health, finance, public-service, and consumer-platform cases use the same comparison fields: user population, data, application authority, applicable duty, possible consequence, scale, fallback, and recovery path. A changed field reopens the related control and evidence claim. Unchanged fields retain their earlier records.
An enterprise assistant may answer a low-impact policy question or expose another customer’s records through the same text interface. The analysis starts with the tenant boundary, retrieval boundary, user identity, eligible records, and any account action that the application can request. A disputed answer is an answer whose correctness or authority is challenged and resolved outside the model.
The NIST Privacy Framework calls for inventories of systems, roles, people, data actions, purposes, data elements, processing environments, and mapped interactions.1 The 2026 OWASP list separates prompt injection, sensitive information disclosure, excessive agency, misinformation, and vector or embedding weaknesses for analysis.2 These frameworks organize the review. They do not show that a weakness exists in the hypothetical assistant or that a proposed control works.
The request path authenticates the employee and filters eligible records before retrieval. The application labels the source and generates an answer. It sends any proposed account action to a separate authorization service. A disputed answer returns to an authoritative record or responsible specialist. This relatively low physical-harm case supplies a comparison point for health information, where an answer can influence care.
Control review. The system of record checks the employee identity and tenant eligibility before returning a document, while the action service checks any account operation separately. Tests report denied cross-tenant requests over all unauthorized pairs and corrected disputed answers over all reviewed answers. Per-request checks, source links, and specialist review add latency and staff cost. Cached records or an alternate connector can bypass the intended route, and these tests cannot establish answer correctness for unreviewed topics. Recovery removes exposed context and revokes affected access. It restores the accepted connector and routes disputed work to the ordinary support process.
crumbs: Part VIII: Adapting controls to change

title: 23  Adapting controls by sector
text:
23.2 Health information assistants
A health assistant changes the stakes when it reads regulated records or appears to direct care. Electronic protected health information means electronic health information within the legal scope of the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA). Clinical authority is permission and responsibility to make or direct a clinical decision. Role-appropriate access limits access to what a person’s assigned work requires.
Within its scope, the HIPAA Security Rule requires administrative, physical, and technical safeguards for electronic protected health information, including access suited to assigned roles.3 The Department of Health and Human Services also requires periodic evaluation after environmental changes such as new technology or newly recognized risks.4 These duties address information security compliance. They do not establish clinical safety or model accuracy.
The hypothetical assistant may summarize an authorized patient’s record for a clinician but cannot diagnose, prescribe, or change an order. Identity, record scope, output labeling, clinical review, correction, and emergency fallback are separate control points. Clinical safety, medical-device scope, and evidence for human review still require use-specific regulation and clinical evaluation. Financial authority provides the next comparison because the system may initiate a reversible or irreversible monetary action.
Control review. The health-record system checks clinician identity, patient relationship, and requested fields. The clinical workflow treats the output as a draft and permits only an authorized clinician to enter an order. Tests report wrong-patient disclosures over all unauthorized patient pairs and unsupported statements over all reviewed summaries. Access checks and clinical review consume time and can delay care. Copied text, stale role data, or use outside the workflow can bypass the controls. Recovery removes the draft and corrects the record. The established clinical or emergency path remains active while staff investigate any affected decision. A passing information-security test does not establish clinical safety or legal compliance.
crumbs: Part VIII: Adapting controls to change

title: 23  Adapting controls by sector
text:
23.3 Financial workflow authority
A financial assistant may classify an alert. Other configurations may prepare or approve a transfer. Those acts need different authority. Transaction authority is permission to initiate, approve, modify, or reverse a financial action. An approval limit sets the maximum value or action class an identity may approve. A reversal is a controlled action that restores an earlier financial state where the rules permit it.
Under the EU AI Act, specified systems used to evaluate a person’s creditworthiness or establish a credit score appear in Annex III, while systems used to detect financial fraud are excluded from that item.5 Classification still depends on intended use, conditions, exceptions, and applicable dates. CSF 2.0 calls for identities to be authenticated and for permissions and authorizations to be defined, enforced, reviewed, and separated by duty.6 Those general outcomes do not define payment rules or reversal rights.
In the hypothetical workflow, the model can explain an alert and prepare a proposed action. The payment system verifies the employee identity, amount, approval limit, separation of duties, and current account state before execution. Logs connect proposal, approval, execution, and reversal. A final case requires current banking, payment, securities, credit, and recordkeeping law for one jurisdiction. The public-service case adds legal effects, explanation, and challenge rights.
Financial action trace. The operating mode is inference with a proposed action, not autonomous execution. Employee E8 asks the assistant to prepare a 14,000 currency-unit transfer after reviewing a fraud alert. The assistant returns the proposed recipient, amount, and reason. The payment system then checks E8’s current identity and 10,000 approval limit. The intermediate decision is a denial followed by escalation to a second authorized employee. The observed result is no transfer and a linked proposal, denial, and escalation record. All values are hypothetical. The trace shows that fluent financial text does not replace transaction authority.
Control review. The payment system checks current identity, amount, approval limit, separated approval, recipient state, and transaction status. It allows, denies, or holds the transfer and records each decision. Tests report unauthorized transfers over all attempted restricted transfers and mistaken denials over all allowed cases. Independent approval and reversal capacity add cost and delay. Shared credentials, a second payment route, or a stale limit can bypass the path. Recovery cancels pending work and reverses eligible transactions. It freezes affected credentials and escalates irreversible loss. A zero-failure test does not establish performance against untested fraud or operational error.
crumbs: Part VIII: Adapting controls to change

title: 23  Adapting controls by sector
text:
23.4 Public service systems
A public service may affect access to benefits or a person’s legal status. It can also influence emergency response or access to justice. Contestability is the ability to challenge a decision and seek correction or review. A legal effect changes a person’s legal rights, duties, or status. Accessibility is the ability of people with differing needs to use the service.
EU AI Act Annex III includes specified uses involving essential public benefits, emergency response, law enforcement, migration, justice, and democratic processes.7 Article 86 provides a limited explanation right for certain decisions based on Annex III high-risk system outputs. It excludes point 2 systems and requires legal or similarly substantial effects that the person considers adverse to health, safety, or fundamental rights.8 Both claims have express conditions, exceptions, and dates. They do not create a general explanation right for every public-sector output.
The hypothetical service keeps the AI output as reviewable input to an authorized decision process. The record identifies the legal basis, evidence, human authority, explanation route, correction path, accessibility needs, and appeal mechanism. This setting emphasizes bounded public authority. The consumer-platform case changes the scale and permits open user access, which shifts attention toward abuse volume and resource limits.
Control review. The case-management system checks the legal basis, required evidence, authorized official, notice, and challenge status before a consequential decision takes effect. It approves, returns, or blocks the decision and preserves the record used. Tests report complete notices and successful challenge routing over all consequential cases in scope, plus decisions corrected after review. Accessibility and human review add time and service cost. Informal channels, incomplete records, or inaccessible notices can defeat the process. Because process evidence does not prove the underlying decision was lawful or correct, recovery pauses the effect where permitted and corrects the record. The person then enters the established review or appeal path.
crumbs: Part VIII: Adapting controls to change

title: 23  Adapting controls by sector
text:
23.5 Consumer platform abuse
An open consumer platform receives high request volume from users whose identity, intent, and content are uncertain. Account abuse is unauthorized or deceptive use of a user account. Impersonation and automated sign-up can occur alongside harmful content. Tool misuse or resource exhaustion may follow even when each request appears minor.
OWASP describes its August 2026 Large Language Model (LLM) Top 10 as a community guide to critical risks in LLM-powered applications.9 Its 2026 list treats excessive agency and unbounded consumption as distinct application risks.10 The list supplies a taxonomy. Prevalence and mitigation effectiveness require separate evidence.
The application can bind rate limits to accounts, devices, payment state, and action classes. It can require stronger verification before consequential actions and give users a reporting path. A hypothetical limit of one hundred requests per hour remains only a design value until load and abuse tests show its effects on legitimate work, attack cost, and service availability. The cross-setting comparison includes this unresolved evidence.
Rate-limit comparison. A hypothetical test replays the same 1,000 ordinary requests and 500 automated abuse requests under limits of 50, 100, and 200 requests per account per hour. The intermediate record separates blocked abuse, blocked ordinary work, queue time, and account switching. At 50, the system blocks more abuse but also blocks a simulated support surge. At 200, it permits more abuse. The test does not choose a universal value because device identity, distributed accounts, and real demand remain uncertain. Its conclusion is that the selected limit needs both abuse and legitimate-work evidence under the platform’s operating conditions.
Control review. The gateway checks account, device, payment state, request rate, and action class before admitting work. It allows, slows, challenges, or blocks the request. The test reports blocked abuse over all simulated abuse and blocked ordinary work over all ordinary requests, together with queue time and infrastructure cost. Stronger checks increase user friction and support demand. Distributed accounts or shared infrastructure can bypass or overwhelm the limit, while the replay cannot estimate real abuse prevalence or prove resilience at a larger scale. Recovery reduces expensive features and protects essential paths. Legitimate users receive a support route.
crumbs: Part VIII: Adapting controls to change

title: 23  Adapting controls by sector
text:
23.6 Comparison across sectors
Each case uses the same system-mapping method, but its assets, permissions, duties, scale, consequences, oversight depth, and recovery evidence differ. A transfer analysis compares what changes when a design enters another setting. Oversight depth combines the frequency, authority, and technical detail of human review.
The AI Risk Management Framework states that risk management is tailored to context and that priorities account for organizational goals, affected people, legal requirements, and available resources.11 CSF 2.0 also states that control choices vary with risk, tolerance, mission, technology, and requirements.12 These sources support tailoring. They do not rank the hypothetical cases or make their controls equivalent.
The method remains constant while each case changes the facts. Enterprise support emphasizes tenant and retrieval separation. Health adds regulated records and clinical boundaries. Finance adds transaction authority and reversal. Public services add legal effects and contestability. Consumer platforms add open access and scale. This analysis shows which assumptions need renewed examination when Chapter 24 introduces exposed devices, distributed training, physical action, persistent agents, and frontier capabilities.
Sector comparison. Each row below changes one condition in the recurring hypothetical organization. It does not establish legal compliance or rank sectors.

The comparison uses the same mapping method while changing the user population, data, authority, consequence, and expected evidence. A control transfers only when those conditions and its mechanism remain the same.
Transfer control. Architecture reviewers compare the source and target setting for data, identity, authority, duty, consequence, operating scale, fallback, and recovery. They accept a control unchanged only when its enforcing component and checked state remain valid. The measure is retested transferred controls over all controls reused in the target setting. Reassessment adds delivery and specialist cost. Superficial similarity can hide a changed legal or physical condition. Because successful transfer of one control does not validate the rest of the design, recovery withdraws the transferred approval and returns the task to the prior setting or manual route.

Note
Chapter checkpoint. Move the enterprise support assistant into the health-information setting. Which parts of the earlier design can remain, and which decision must be reopened first?
Answer. Identity checks, source links, retrieval filtering, and a disputed-answer route can remain as candidate controls. Their tests must use health-record roles and data. Authority must be reviewed first. An employee-support answer cannot become clinical direction merely because the same model and retrieval pattern are used. The organization needs current legal scope, clinical evaluation, authorized oversight, correction, and emergency fallback before approving the changed use.
